primeiro-emprego-irlanda-emergency-tax.en_title: First Job in Ireland: How to Avoid Emergency Tax
primeiro-emprego-irlanda-emergency-tax.en_excerpt: Register your first job with Revenue, use myAccount and check your Tax Credit Certificate.
primeiro-emprego-irlanda-emergency-tax.en_content:
Meta description: Just started your first job in Ireland? See how to register the job with Revenue, use myAccount, avoid Emergency Tax and check your Tax Credit Certificate.

Suggested URL: /guias/primeiro-emprego-irlanda-emergency-tax/

Introduction

Your first payslip can carry more tax than expected when Revenue cannot yet give your employer the correct Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN). This is called Emergency Tax.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians in their first job in Ireland, especially those who have just obtained their PPSN and have not yet registered their first job with Revenue.

Step by step

  • Have your PPSN.
  • Create or access Revenue myAccount.
  • In PAYE Services, use Add Job or Pension Details to register the first job.
  • Have your PPSN, the employer’s Tax Registration Number and the start date to hand.
  • Give your PPSN to the employer and check that the job appears in myAccount.
  • Check the Tax Credit Certificate.
  • If Emergency Tax applied, follow Revenue’s instructions; once the correct RPN is available, amounts overpaid can be corrected through payroll under the applicable rules.

Documents and information needed

  • PPSN.
  • Employer details and Tax Registration Number.
  • Start date.
  • An active myAccount.
  • Tax Credit Certificate, when available.

Costs and fees

There is no fee to register a job in myAccount.

Timelines and important dates

Register as soon as possible, ideally before the first payment.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Assuming the employer always registers the first job.
  • Not giving the employer your PPSN.
  • Not checking the TCC and the jobs listed in myAccount.
  • Confusing Emergency Tax with a fine.

Official sources

  • Revenue - Starting your first job
  • Revenue - what to do
  • Revenue - Emergency Tax
  • Revenue - getting off Emergency Tax

Useful links

  • Revenue - Starting your first job
  • Revenue - what to do
  • Revenue - Emergency Tax
  • Revenue - getting off Emergency Tax

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to register every job in myAccount?

For the first job in the State, Revenue advises the worker to register it. For later jobs the employer normally reports the employment.

What happens if I do not register?

The employer may not be able to obtain the required RPN and may apply Emergency Tax.

When does the TCC appear?

Revenue states that after registration the TCC can be available within up to two working days.

Is Emergency Tax refunded?

Amounts overpaid can be corrected once the correct RPN is available, under Revenue’s rules.

sole-trader-autonomo-irlanda-brasileiros.en_title: How to Work as a Sole Trader in Ireland
sole-trader-autonomo-irlanda-brasileiros.en_excerpt: Sole trader tax registration, self-assessment and how ROS is used in Ireland.
sole-trader-autonomo-irlanda-brasileiros.en_content:
Meta description: See how to set up sole trader tax registration in Ireland, when to register for Income Tax, how ROS is used and what to keep in mind.

Suggested URL: /guias/sole-trader-autonomo-irlanda-brasileiros/

Introduction

For freelancers and professionals who work for themselves, the tax route is usually that of the sole trader and self-assessment. This is different from incorporating a limited company.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians in Ireland who intend to provide services on their own account or start a sole activity.

Step by step

  • Confirm that your working relationship really is self-employed.
  • Have a PPSN: Revenue states that it is needed before the sole trader tax registration.
  • Register for Income Tax according to your situation, using myAccount or the channel indicated by Revenue.
  • After registration, use ROS where required for returns and payments.
  • If you trade under a name different from your own, check the business name registration at the CRO.
  • Keep records of income, expenses and documents from the start.
  • Check additional obligations such as VAT or Employer PAYE where they apply.

Documents and information needed

  • PPSN.
  • Start date and activity details.
  • Expected turnover information.
  • Records of income and expenses.
  • Additional details for VAT/PAYE, if applicable.

Costs and fees

Revenue does not present the sole trader tax registration as a set-up fee; other registrations or licences may have their own costs.

Timelines and important dates

Returns and payments follow the tax calendar. Self-assessment has annual Pay and File dates: check the year in question.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Confusing a sole trader with a limited company.
  • Starting to invoice without checking the tax registration you need.
  • Not keeping adequate documents and records.
  • Using thresholds and dates from a previous year.

Official sources

  • Revenue - sole trader
  • Revenue - self-assessment
  • Companies Registration Office

Useful links

  • Revenue - self-assessment

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a PPSN?

Yes. Revenue states that a PPSN is needed before the sole trader tax registration.

Do I need to use ROS?

After registration, Revenue states that ROS is used for business-related returns and payments where applicable.

Are there income limits for self-assessment?

Yes. Revenue sets criteria and limits for non-PAYE income: check the current figures for the year in question.

Is a sole trader the same as a company?

No. A sole trader is an individual activity; a company is a separate legal entity.

hse-irlanda-gp-out-of-hours-injury-unit-.en_title: HSE in Ireland: When to See a GP, GP Out-of-Hours, Injury Unit or Emergency Department
hse-irlanda-gp-out-of-hours-injury-unit-.en_excerpt: Where to seek medical care in Ireland, what it costs and when to call 112 or 999.
hse-irlanda-gp-out-of-hours-injury-unit-.en_content:
Meta description: Understand where to seek medical care in Ireland: GP, GP out-of-hours, Injury Unit and Emergency Department, including costs and when to call 112 or 999.

Suggested URL: /guias/hse-irlanda-gp-out-of-hours-injury-unit-emergency-department/

Introduction

Ireland’s urgent care system can be different from Brazil’s. Not every situation needs an Emergency Department. The HSE advises choosing the service according to the severity and type of problem.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians living in Ireland who need to know where to seek care when their GP is closed, or when an injury or emergency happens.

Step by step

  • For non-urgent problems, see your GP during normal opening hours.
  • If the GP is closed and you need urgent care, use the GP out-of-hours service; the HSE states that it normally works by phone with triage.
  • For recent non-life-threatening injuries that are unlikely to need admission, check whether there is an Injury Unit suitable for your age and region.
  • Go to an Emergency Department for serious or potentially life-threatening situations.
  • If there is a risk to life or a need for urgent treatment, call 112 or 999.
  • Before you leave, check the HSE finder for the unit, opening hours, the ages it treats and any disruptions.

Official links: Find urgent or emergency care - HSE · Find a GP

Documents and information needed

  • Medical Card or GP Visit Card, if you have one.
  • Information about your medication and relevant conditions.
  • Identity document, when requested.

Costs and fees

The HSE currently states €75 for an Injury Unit and €100 for an Emergency Department, with exemptions in situations such as holding a Medical Card or being referred. Confirm the amounts before publication.

Timelines and important dates

There is no deadline in an emergency. In a serious situation do not wait: call 112 or 999.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Going to an Emergency Department for any symptom.
  • Using an Injury Unit for problems it does not treat.
  • Not checking the unit’s age range and opening hours.
  • Assuming the cost is always the same.

Official sources

  • HSE - Urgent and emergency care
  • HSE - find care
  • HSE - GP out-of-hours
  • HSE - Injury Unit

Useful links

  • HSE - Urgent and emergency care

  • HSE - GP out-of-hours
  • HSE - Injury Unit

Frequently asked questions

When should I use an Injury Unit?

For recent, non-life-threatening injuries such as some fractures, sprains, cuts and minor burns.

When should I go to an Emergency Department?

For serious or potentially life-threatening problems; if life is at risk, call 112 or 999.

Is GP out-of-hours walk-in?

The HSE states that it normally works by phone with triage.

How much does an Injury Unit cost?

The amount currently stated by the HSE is €75, with some exemptions. Confirm before publishing.

Important notice

ehic-irlanda-brasileiros-residentes.en_title: EHIC in Ireland: How Resident Brazilians Can Get the European Health Insurance Card
ehic-irlanda-brasileiros-residentes.en_excerpt: Who can apply for an EHIC in Ireland, what the HSE asks for and where it is valid.
ehic-irlanda-brasileiros-residentes.en_content:
Meta description: Find out who can apply for an EHIC in Ireland, which documents the HSE asks for, where it is valid and why it is not travel insurance.

Suggested URL: /guias/ehic-irlanda-brasileiros-residentes/

Introduction

The EHIC is useful for Brazilians living in Ireland who travel around Europe. It can give access to necessary public healthcare during temporary stays, subject to the rules of the country visited.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians living in Ireland who plan to travel to EU, EEA or Swiss countries.

Step by step

  • Confirm your eligibility: the HSE states that people living in Ireland can apply if they intend to live here for at least one year, subject to the applicable criteria.
  • Have proof of residence and proof of your PPSN ready, where they are required.
  • Apply online – the option the HSE describes as the fastest – or use the official postal/email channels.
  • Each family member needs their own card where applicable.
  • If you are travelling in less than 10 days, look at the urgent option and the Provisional Replacement Certificate.
  • Take the card with you and do not treat the EHIC as travel insurance.

Documents and information needed

  • Proof of residence in Ireland.
  • Proof of your PPSN.
  • Personal details of the applicants and dependants.
  • Any additional documents required by the HSE.

Costs and fees

The HSE provides the EHIC application service; confirm the current conditions at the time you apply.

Timelines and important dates

If the trip is coming up, use the online option and check the urgent procedure described by the HSE.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Thinking the EHIC covers private treatment.
  • Thinking the EHIC covers repatriation.
  • Using the EHIC for planned treatment.
  • Not checking the destination’s co-payment rules.

Official sources

  • HSE - EHIC
  • HSE - apply for an EHIC
  • HSE - using the EHIC

Useful links

Frequently asked questions

Can a Brazilian get an Irish EHIC?

Brazilian nationality is not the only criterion. Eligibility depends on your residence situation and the HSE rules.

Where is the EHIC valid?

The HSE states that it is accepted in EU, EEA and Swiss countries, under the local rules.

Does the EHIC cover a private hospital?

No. The HSE states that it relates to necessary public care.

Does the EHIC replace travel insurance?

No. The HSE expressly states that it does not replace travel insurance.

reconhecer-diploma-brasileiro-na-irlanda.en_title: How to Get a Brazilian Diploma Recognised in Ireland: NARIC and QQI Guide
reconhecer-diploma-brasileiro-na-irlanda.en_excerpt: How to compare a Brazilian qualification with the Irish NFQ and what the limits are.
reconhecer-diploma-brasileiro-na-irlanda.en_content:
Meta description: See how to use NARIC Ireland/QQI to compare a Brazilian qualification with the National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) and what the limits of that comparison are.

Suggested URL: /guias/reconhecer-diploma-brasileiro-na-irlanda-naric-qqi/

Introduction

People who arrive with a Brazilian degree, postgraduate degree or other qualification often need to explain the level of their diploma to employers or institutions. NARIC Ireland, operated by the QQI, provides academic guidance through comparability statements.

Official links: QQI guidance on recognising foreign qualifications

Who this guide is for

Brazilians with diplomas or academic qualifications obtained in Brazil who need to present their education in Ireland.

Step by step

  • Go to the NARIC Ireland Foreign Qualifications Database.
  • Select Brazil and look for the type and title of the qualification.
  • If it is in the database, download the Comparability Statement.
  • Read the comparable level in the Irish NFQ and the notes in the statement.
  • If it is not in the database, use the QQI Qualifications Recognition Advice service.
  • Present the statement to the employer or institution when it is requested.
  • For a regulated profession, also check the professional body: the NARIC statement is not a professional licence.

Documents and information needed

  • Official name of the qualification.
  • The institution that awarded the diploma.
  • Academic documents and translations, when required by the receiving body.

Costs and fees

The NARIC database is provided free of charge by the QQI. Translations, certifications and professional processes may have their own costs.

Timelines and important dates

There is no universal deadline: apply in advance if the statement is needed for an application.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Treating a comparability statement as a professional licence.
  • Assuming every diploma will automatically be in the database.
  • Using an old statement without checking the current version.
  • Ignoring the regulator for a regulated profession.

Official sources

  • QQI - recognition of foreign qualifications
  • NARIC - Foreign Qualifications Database
  • QQI QHelp - Recognition Advice

Useful links

  • QQI - recognition of foreign qualifications
  • NARIC - Foreign Qualifications Database
  • QQI QHelp - Recognition Advice

Frequently asked questions

Does NARIC recognise my diploma for any job?

No. The QQI explains that the information is academic guidance and does not in itself give access to a job, a regulated profession or a course.

What if my diploma is not in the database?

You can request general guidance from the QQI.

Do I need to translate my diploma?

It depends on the institution, employer or body that requests the document.

Is a comparability statement mandatory?

Not necessarily: it is an official tool that may be requested or useful depending on the process.

leap-card-irlanda-como-usar.en_title: Leap Card in Ireland: How to Use the Transport Card and Pay Less
leap-card-irlanda-como-usar.en_excerpt: How the TFI Leap Card works, where to use it, how to top it up and what to do if you lose it.
leap-card-irlanda-como-usar.en_content:

Suggested URL: /guias/leap-card-irlanda-como-usar/

Introduction

For people who use buses, the Luas, DART and other services, the TFI Leap Card is a practical way to pay for journeys and can offer lower fares than cash in many situations.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians living, studying or working in Ireland who use public transport regularly.

Step by step

  • Choose the type of Leap Card that suits your situation.
  • Buy the card through an official channel and, where possible, register it.
  • Add Travel Credit or the appropriate product.
  • Use the card according to the service’s tap on/tap off rules.
  • Check fares, zones and fare capping on the current TFI page.
  • Register the card to make replacement or refunds easier where allowed.
  • Use the app/online account to check your balance and transactions.

Documents and information needed

  • For a standard adult card there is normally no complex documentation.
  • Discounted cards have specific eligibility and evidence requirements.

Costs and fees

Fares depend on the passenger, zone and service. TFI keeps the current fare tables: avoid publishing figures without checking the page on the day you publish.

Timelines and important dates

There is no general deadline; validity rules depend on the product.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Not registering the card.
  • Assuming every line has the same fare or capping.
  • Confusing Adult, Young Adult and Student cards.
  • Using old fares from third parties.

  • TFI - Fare Zones

Where can I use the Leap Card?

TFI states that it works on many services in the network, including buses, the Luas, DART and some rail services.

Is it worth registering?

Yes. TFI recommends registering the card because unregistered cards cannot be replaced or refunded if lost.

Is there a daily cap?

Yes, in certain zones and services. TFI applies fare capping.

Do all cards have the same discounts?

No. There are different types, such as Adult, Young Adult/Student and Child, with their own rules.

learner-permit-theory-test-irlanda-cnh-b.en_title: Brazilian Driving Licence in Ireland: When You Need the Theory Test and Learner Permit
learner-permit-theory-test-irlanda-cnh-b.en_excerpt: The route for Brazilians who cannot exchange their licence: theory test, learner permit, EDT and driving test.
learner-permit-theory-test-irlanda-cnh-b.en_content:
Meta description: Understand the route for Brazilians who cannot exchange their foreign licence: theory test, learner permit, EDT and driving test.

Suggested URL: /guias/learner-permit-theory-test-irlanda-cnh-brasileira/

Introduction

Exchanging a foreign licence depends on exchange agreements. When the licence cannot be exchanged, the driver may have to follow the Irish process to obtain the licence.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians with a foreign driving licence who need to understand the route to an Irish licence when no exchange applies.

Step by step

  • First check with the NDLS whether your licence is eligible for exchange.
  • If you need the learner driver route, pass the Driver Theory Test for the correct category.
  • Apply for the first learner permit through the NDLS, noting identity, address, ordinary residence, PPSN and reports where applicable.
  • If you hold a full licence from a country with no exchange agreement, check whether you are entitled to the Reduced EDT Programme.
  • For the first learner permit, the RSA states it must be held for at least six months and the required training completed before the driving test.
  • Book the driving test once all the requirements are met.

Documents and information needed

  • Passport or an accepted document.
  • PPSN.
  • Proof of address where required.
  • Proof of ordinary residence where applicable.
  • Theory test certificate.
  • Eye or medical report, if required.

Costs and fees

The theory test, learner permit, lessons and driving test each have their own costs. Check RSA/NDLS for the current amounts.

Timelines and important dates

The RSA states that the learner permit must be applied for within two years of passing the theory test; after that the certificate expires.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Driving unaccompanied with a learner permit.
  • Booking the theory test on an unofficial site.
  • Ignoring the six months for the first learner permit.
  • Assuming a Brazilian licence is automatically exchangeable.

It depends on the exchange rules in force. Check with the NDLS before starting the process.

Do I need to take the theory test?

For the first learner permit, the RSA states that you must pass the theory test for the category.

How long do I hold a learner permit?

For the first learner permit, the RSA states six months, in addition to the required training.

Can I drive on my own?

No. The learner permit rules require an accompanying driver according to the category and the applicable conditions.

assistencia-juridica-legal-aid-irlanda-b.en_title: Legal Aid in Ireland: How to Apply for Civil Legal Aid
assistencia-juridica-legal-aid-irlanda-b.en_excerpt: How Civil Legal Aid works, who can apply, the means test and possible contributions.
assistencia-juridica-legal-aid-irlanda-b.en_content:
Meta description: See how Civil Legal Aid from the Legal Aid Board works, who can apply, how the means test works and what contributions may apply.

Suggested URL: /guias/assistencia-juridica-legal-aid-irlanda-brasileiros/

Introduction

Legal problems are harder when you are still learning the Irish system. The Legal Aid Board provides civil legal advice and representation services for people who meet the financial criteria and the merits test.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians in Ireland with a civil legal matter who want to check access to the Legal Aid Board.

Step by step

  • Check that the matter is within the scope of Civil Legal Aid. Criminal matters are not covered by the Civil Legal Aid Act.
  • Check your possible financial eligibility. The Board currently states disposable income below €18,000, and also takes assets and circumstances into account.
  • Use the financial eligibility indicator as a first guide, without treating it as a guarantee.
  • Prepare proof of income, expenses and assets.
  • Submit the application online or go to a Law Centre.
  • Wait for the financial and merits assessment; there may be a waiting list.
  • Check the contribution that applies and any exemptions.

Official links: Apply for Civil Legal Aid · Check financial eligibility

Documents and information needed

  • Address and PPSN.
  • Proof of income and benefits.
  • Proof of expenses.
  • Information about assets and debts.
  • Documents relating to the legal problem.

Costs and fees

The Board currently states a minimum contribution of €30 for advice, plus contributions for representation depending on the situation. Exemptions and special rules exist.

Timelines and important dates

Court deadlines keep running while you seek assistance. Do not let a deadline expire while waiting for a place.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Confusing the Legal Aid Board with free help for any issue.
  • Not sending financial evidence.
  • Letting a court deadline pass.
  • Assuming the calculator guarantees approval.

Nationality by itself neither guarantees nor prevents it. The type of case, your financial situation and the merits test are what matter.

What is the income limit?

The Board currently states disposable income below €18,000, plus asset criteria and the specifics of the case.

Is it always free?

No. In many cases there is a contribution; exemptions exist.

How long does it take?

It varies by Law Centre and there may be a waiting list; the Board publishes statistics.

casamento-registro-nascimento-irlanda-br.en_title: Marriage and Birth Registration in Ireland: A Guide for Brazilian Families
casamento-registro-nascimento-irlanda-br.en_excerpt: How to register a birth and how civil marriage works, including notice and fees.
casamento-registro-nascimento-irlanda-br.en_content:
Meta description: Understand how to register a birth in Ireland and how civil marriage works, including notice, documents, fees and the extra steps for foreign nationals.

Suggested URL: /guias/casamento-registro-nascimento-irlanda-brasileiros/

Introduction

Having children and getting married in Ireland involve civil registration procedures that can be different from the Brazilian ones. The General Register Office and the civil registration services hold the official information.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians who have children in Ireland, plan to marry in the country, or need civil registration certificates.

Step by step

  • For a birth, register the child within the official deadline: gov.ie states a maximum of three months after the birth.
  • Use the Civil Registration Service and check the online option available.
  • Request the birth certificate when you need it for school, a passport or other processes.
  • For a marriage, give at least three months notice to the civil registration service.
  • Book the marriage notification appointment and both partners must attend.
  • Prepare passports, birth certificates, proof of address and PPS Numbers, plus special documents where applicable.
  • If one partner is a foreign national, check the interview, proof of immigration status, translation and interpreter requirements where they apply.
  • After the ceremony, follow the registration procedure and request the marriage certificate if you need it.

Documents and information needed

  • For a birth: the information and documents requested by the Civil Registration Service.
  • For a marriage: passport, birth certificate, proof of address, PPSN and specific documents.
  • Translations where documents are not in English or Irish.

Costs and fees

The marriage notification fee is a non-refundable €200. The marriage registration itself is free, but certificates have fees. Confirm the current amounts.

Timelines and important dates

Birth: up to three months. Marriage: at least three months notice before the ceremony.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Leaving the birth registration too late.
  • Booking a marriage without allowing for the three months notice.
  • Bringing copies without the originals where they are required.
  • Forgetting translations or the extra documentation for foreign nationals.

gov.ie currently states a maximum of three months after the birth.

How far in advance do I notify a marriage?

The general rule is three months notice, given in person to the civil registration service.

Do foreign nationals need an interview?

gov.ie states that an interview is required when one of the partners is a foreign national, among other situations.

How much does the marriage notice cost?

The notification fee is currently €200 and non-refundable; registration and certificates have their own rules.

reclamar-banco-seguro-servico-financeiro.en_title: How to Complain About a Bank, Insurer or Financial Service in Ireland
reclamar-banco-seguro-servico-financeiro.en_excerpt: Check that a firm is authorised and complain about a bank, insurer or financial service.
reclamar-banco-seguro-servico-financeiro.en_content:
Meta description: Learn how to check that a financial firm is authorised in Ireland and how to complain about a bank, insurer, credit provider or other financial service.

Suggested URL: /guias/reclamar-banco-seguro-servico-financeiro-irlanda/

Introduction

Problems with a bank, insurer, credit, investment or payments can be hard in another language. The Central Bank of Ireland keeps the register of authorised firms, and the FSPO offers an independent route for eligible complaints.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians who use banks, insurance, credit, investments, payments or other financial services in Ireland.

Step by step

  • Before you sign up, look the firm up in the Central Bank Register of Authorised Firms.
  • Confirm the legal name, because a firm may trade under a different name.
  • If there is a problem, make a formal complaint directly to the firm: firms must have a complaints procedure.
  • Keep the contract, statements, emails, letters, receipts and call logs.
  • If the reply does not resolve it, check whether the case can go to the FSPO.
  • Use the FSPO form and attach the relevant documents and the final response letter where applicable.
  • If you suspect an unauthorised firm, report it to the Central Bank of Ireland.

Documents and information needed

  • Contract/policy.
  • Statements and receipts.
  • Communications with the firm.
  • Final Response Letter where applicable.
  • Account or policy details.

Costs and fees

The FSPO states that its service is free. The Central Bank register is also public and free.

Timelines and important dates

The FSPO states that the firm can take up to 40 working days in its internal process. There are time limits for referring a case to the Ombudsman: check them before you wait.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Sending money without checking authorisation.
  • Complaining without keeping evidence.
  • Skipping the formal complaint to the provider.
  • Confusing an individual complaint with a systemic regulatory report.

Official sources

  • Central Bank - registers
  • Central Bank - authorised firms
  • FSPO - complain to your provider
  • FSPO - complaint form

Useful links

Frequently asked questions

How do I check whether a firm is authorised?

Search the Register of Authorised Firms and confirm the legal name.

Can I complain to the Central Bank to get my money back?

Generally not. For individual complaints the normal route is the firm and then, where applicable, the FSPO.

Does the FSPO charge?

The FSPO states that the service is free.

Do I need to keep evidence?

Yes. The FSPO recommends documents such as contracts, statements, emails and letters.

reclamar-servico-publico-irlanda-ombudsm.en_title: How to Complain About a Public Service in Ireland: When to Use the Ombudsman
reclamar-servico-publico-irlanda-ombudsm.en_excerpt: Complain about a government department, local authority or public service in Ireland.
reclamar-servico-publico-irlanda-ombudsm.en_content:
Meta description: See how to complain about a government department, local authority or public service in Ireland and when the Office of the Ombudsman can examine the complaint.

Suggested URL: /guias/reclamar-servico-publico-irlanda-ombudsman/

Introduction

If a Brazilian has a problem with an Irish public service, there is a formal route. The Office of the Ombudsman can investigate certain complaints against government departments, local authorities and the HSE.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians who had a problem with a government department, local authority or the HSE and could not resolve it through the normal channel.

Step by step

  • Identify the body that made the decision or provided the service.
  • First complain directly to the body, explaining what happened and what you expect to be corrected.
  • Keep references, emails, letters, names, dates and documents.
  • If the reply does not resolve it, check whether the Ombudsman can handle that type of complaint.
  • Submit the complaint within the applicable time limit. The Ombudsman states a general rule of 12 months, save for special circumstances.
  • Do not use the Ombudsman for matters outside its remit, such as many complaints against private companies, banks or An Garda Síochána.

Documents and information needed

  • Description of the facts.
  • The body’s response.
  • References and case numbers.
  • Related documents, letters and emails.

Costs and fees

No fee is stated for making a complaint to the Ombudsman.

Timelines and important dates

Published general rule: 12 months, save for very special circumstances.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Going straight to the Ombudsman without trying to resolve it with the body.
  • Waiting more than 12 months without checking whether you can complain.
  • Sending a complaint without a timeline and evidence.
  • Using the Ombudsman for an FSPO or WRC matter.

Official sources

  • Ombudsman - how to complain
  • Ombudsman - making a complaint

Useful links

  • Ombudsman - how to complain
  • Ombudsman - making a complaint

Frequently asked questions

Can I go straight to the Ombudsman?

In general, try to resolve it with the public service first.

Does the Ombudsman deal with private companies?

Not in general: the body itself lists several categories that are outside its remit.

Is there a deadline?

The published general rule is 12 months, save for very special circumstances.

Is the HSE included?

Yes. The Ombudsman states that it investigates certain complaints about HSE services.

Official links: Make a complaint to the Ombudsman

Last checked

Important notice

For information only; it does not replace legal advice.

checklist-viagem-internacional-irlanda-b.en_title: First International Trip with an IRP: Documents Checklist for Brazilians
checklist-viagem-internacional-irlanda-b.en_excerpt: A practical checklist before travelling: passport, IRP, destination, return and emergency documents.
checklist-viagem-internacional-irlanda-b.en_content:
Meta description: A practical checklist for Brazilians resident in Ireland before travelling: passport, IRP, destination, return and emergency documents.

Suggested URL: /guias/checklist-viagem-internacional-irlanda-brasileiros-irp/

Introduction

This guide turns the official travel and return rules into a simple check before departure. It complements the guide on the IRP and travel, with a focus on planning.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians resident in Ireland who are travelling to Brazil, Europe or another country and want to reduce the risk of documentation problems.

Step by step

  • Check the validity of your passport.
  • Check the validity of your IRP and that the details are correct.
  • Check the entry rules of the destination on the relevant official source.
  • Check whether the airline requires any additional documentation.
  • Save digital copies of your passport, IRP, insurance and bookings.
  • If the IRP is lost or you have no valid card, contact the ISD before you leave.
  • After you return, check whether your address, passport or other details changed and need to be reported to the ISD.

Official links: Irish Immigration Service

Documents and information needed

  • Passport.
  • IRP.
  • Travel insurance, if purchased.
  • Destination entry documents.
  • Travel confirmations and emergency contacts.

Costs and fees

There is no cost to do the checklist. Visa, insurance and other document costs depend on the destination.

Timelines and important dates

Do the check at least a few days before you travel and again on the eve of departure.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Leaving the check until the airport.
  • Assuming the IRP replaces a destination visa.
  • Travelling without copies of your documents.

Official sources

  • ISD - Travel and Re-Entry Visas
  • DFA - Travel Advice

Useful links

  • ISD - Travel and Re-Entry Visas
  • DFA - Travel Advice

Frequently asked questions

Does the IRP replace a passport?

No. The IRP and the passport have different functions.

Does the IRP guarantee entry to the destination?

No. Check with the destination country.

What do I do if I lose the IRP?

Check the ISD emergency procedure before travelling.

Do I need travel insurance?

The EHIC does not replace travel insurance: for travel, consider cover that matches the destination and your situation.

Official links: Official rules for travel and re-entry with an IRP · Department of Foreign Affairs travel advice

Last checked

Information checked on 18 August 2026. Reconfirm fees, deadlines, forms, occupation lists, opening hours and procedures before publication and before advising readers on a specific case.

Important notice

Informative checklist; always confirm the official rules for your destination and situation.

reclamacao-trabalhista-wrc-irlanda-brasi.en_title: How to File and Track a Workplace Complaint with the WRC
reclamacao-trabalhista-wrc-irlanda-brasi.en_excerpt: How to file a complaint or dispute with the Workplace Relations Commission and what to keep.
reclamacao-trabalhista-wrc-irlanda-brasi.en_content:
Meta description: Understand how to file a workplace complaint or dispute with the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) and what to keep before starting the process.

Suggested URL: /guias/reclamacao-trabalhista-wrc-irlanda-brasileiros/

Introduction

Even with a general guide on employment rights, many Brazilians need practical guidance on what to do once the problem has happened. The WRC provides an eComplaint Portal for referring certain complaints and disputes.

Who this guide is for

Brazilians who work or worked in Ireland and need to understand the official route for a workplace complaint.

Step by step

  • Identify which right or obligation may have been breached and check the WRC information.
  • Collect the contract, payslips, timesheets, messages, emails, internal policies and other documents.
  • Where possible, try to resolve the issue with the employer and record what was requested and answered.
  • Use the WRC eComplaint Portal when the matter falls within the WRC’s remit.
  • Complete the complaint with facts, dates and relevant documents, without exaggerating or leaving out information.
  • After submitting, follow the WRC communications. The case may proceed to inspection, conciliation or adjudication depending on the nature of the dispute.

Documents and information needed

  • Contract of employment.
  • Payslips.
  • Timesheets.
  • Emails and messages.
  • Documents or responses from the employer.

Costs and fees

The WRC provides the eComplaint Portal: check the official page to see whether there is any specific cost for your procedure.

Timelines and important dates

Complaint time limits vary with the legislation and the type of case. Do not wait until close to the limit; confirm the applicable deadline directly with the WRC.

Common mistakes and points to note

  • Not keeping evidence.
  • Missing the applicable deadline.
  • Sending a generic complaint with no dates or facts.
  • Confusing the WRC with the Labour Court or another body.

Official sources

  • WRC - Make a Complaint / Refer a Dispute
  • WRC - main website

Useful links

  • WRC - Make a Complaint / Refer a Dispute
  • WRC - main website

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to complain to the employer first?

Not every procedure requires exactly the same step, but trying to resolve it internally can help and should be checked according to the type of complaint.

Can I submit the complaint online?

The WRC provides an eComplaint Portal for the complaints and disputes it covers.

Which evidence should I keep?

The contract, payslips, timesheets, emails, messages and the employer’s responses are useful examples.

How long do I have?

The time limit depends on the legislation and the type of complaint. Check with the WRC for your case.

Official links: File a complaint in the WRC eComplaint Portal · Official guidance on making a complaint

beneficios-pais-solteiros-irlanda.en_title: Benefits for Lone Parents in Ireland: Payments, Tax and Other Supports
beneficios-pais-solteiros-irlanda.en_excerpt: Which payments, tax credits and supports may exist for lone parents in Ireland.
beneficios-pais-solteiros-irlanda.en_content:
Raising a child on your own is already a big challenge. For anyone living in Ireland as an immigrant, understanding which benefits, payments and supports may be available can be even more complicated.

Ireland has different schemes for families with children, but there is no single “single mother” or “single father” benefit that automatically entitles everyone to all the supports.

What are the main benefits for lone parents?

  • One-Parent Family Payment (OFP)
  • Jobseeker’s Transitional Payment (JST)
  • Child Benefit
  • Working Family Payment (WFP)
  • Single Person Child Carer Credit (SPCCC)
  • Domiciliary Care Allowance, where the child meets the criteria
  • Carer’s Allowance or Carer’s Benefit in certain situations
  • housing and income supports, depending on your financial situation

Official links: Explore and start other payments on MyWelfare

1. One-Parent Family Payment

The One-Parent Family Payment (OFP) is one of the main payments for people raising children without the support of a partner. It is generally a payment subject to a means test, where certain income and resources are assessed.

The rules depend on your individual situation and include requirements linked to the child’s age, income and family situation.

Official links: Check the One-Parent Family Payment

Can I work and still receive the OFP?

The fact that you work does not necessarily mean the payment is automatically cancelled. The OFP is subject to an income assessment under the scheme rules.

What about child maintenance?

The rules on child maintenance have changed. Do not use old information found on blogs or videos without checking the current rule directly with the Department of Social Protection.

2. Jobseeker’s Transitional Payment

The Jobseeker’s Transitional Payment (JST) was created to help certain lone parents who stop receiving the One-Parent Family Payment because their youngest child reaches the OFP age limit. The JST has its own eligibility rules.

Official links: Check the Jobseeker’s Transitional Payment

3. Child Benefit

Child Benefit is different from the OFP. It is a payment linked to the child and can be received by families who meet the scheme criteria. A lone parent should check Child Benefit even if they are not entitled to the OFP.

Official links: Apply for Child Benefit · Check Child Benefit

4. Working Family Payment

If you work but your family income is relatively low, the Working Family Payment (WFP) is worth looking at. The scheme is for workers with children whose family income is below the limit that applies to their family size.

A common mistake is to think: “I work, so I am not entitled to any benefit.” That is not necessarily true.

Official links: Apply for the Working Family Payment · Check and apply for the Working Family Payment

5. Single Person Child Carer Credit

The Single Person Child Carer Credit (SPCCC) is a tax credit administered by Revenue. For 2026 the credit is €1,900 per year. Anyone who qualifies may also have an additional band of income taxed at 20%, under Revenue’s rules.

Official links: Check and claim the SPCCC

Who can apply?

You must meet Revenue’s conditions to be considered eligible and have a qualifying child. There are specific rules for separated and widowed people and for those who share the care of the child.

How do I apply?

If you are PAYE you can claim through Revenue myAccount, under Manage your tax for the current year, PAYE Services, Claim tax credits and You and your family. If you are self-employed, follow Revenue’s instructions for ROS.

6. Domiciliary Care Allowance

If your child has a disability and needs significantly more care and attention than a child of the same age would normally need, another important payment may apply: Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA). This payment is not exclusive to lone parents and has its own criteria.

7. Carer’s Allowance and Carer’s Benefit

If you have to stop working or significantly reduce your hours to care for someone who needs full-time care, there may be carer-related payments. They are not exclusive to lone parents and have their own requirements.

8. Support to return to work or start a business

The Back to Work Enterprise Allowance (BTWEA) may be relevant for some people who receive certain social payments and want to start a business. There are eligibility requirements, benefit duration rules and prior approval of the business.

9. Housing supports

Depending on your income and family situation, it may be worth checking the Housing Assistance Payment (HAP), social housing and other housing-related supports. There is no general rule saying that all lone parents get automatic priority in any housing scheme.

10. If I am unemployed

If you are a lone parent who has lost their job, the options may depend on the child’s age, PRSI record, income and other circumstances. Jobseeker’s Transitional Payment, Jobseeker’s Allowance, Jobseeker’s Benefit or other payments may be available.

What should a Brazilian have ready?

  • PPS Number
  • identity document
  • proof of address
  • bank details
  • the child’s documents and PPS Number
  • salary and payslips
  • information about other income
  • information about custody, separation or divorce, where relevant

Checklist: am I a lone parent in Ireland?

  • Do I have a PPS Number?
  • Does my child have a PPS Number?
  • Am I receiving Child Benefit?
  • Can I apply for the One-Parent Family Payment?
  • Should I check the Jobseeker’s Transitional Payment?
  • Could my income qualify me for the Working Family Payment?
  • Can I claim the Single Person Child Carer Credit?
  • Does my child have needs that may qualify for the Domiciliary Care Allowance?
  • Do I need to check Carer’s Allowance or Carer’s Benefit?
  • Am I entitled to any housing support?
  • Is my family and tax situation up to date?

Frequently asked questions

Is there a specific single mother benefit in Ireland?

The One-Parent Family Payment is one of the main payments for people raising children without the support of a partner, but it is not the only support available.

Can a single father also receive it?

Yes. The schemes are not exclusively for women. Eligibility depends on the rules of each payment.

Can I work and receive benefits?

In some cases, yes. How income is treated varies by payment.

What is the SPCCC?

It is the Single Person Child Carer Credit, a tax credit administered by Revenue. In 2026 the credit is €1,900.

What if I share custody - can I receive the SPCCC?

There may be a possibility of a secondary claimant, but there are specific rules about the days the child lives with each parent and about transferring the credit.

Do I have to report a change in my family situation?

Yes. Changes such as marriage, reconciliation or living together can affect certain payments and tax credits. Check and report to the responsible body when needed.

Official sources

  • Department of Social Protection
  • Citizens Information - Parenting alone
  • Revenue - Single Person Child Carer Credit
  • Revenue - Tax rates, bands and reliefs
  • Revenue

Last checked

Information checked: 28 August 2026.

Social welfare payments and tax credits can change with the Budget, new laws, changes in rates, income limits, residence rules and eligibility criteria. Always confirm the information directly with the Department of Social Protection, Revenue or Citizens Information.

Notice: This guide is for information only. Social welfare payments, taxes and eligibility criteria depend on individual circumstances. This information does not constitute personalised legal, tax or financial advice.

violencia-domestica-irlanda-onde-encontr.en_title: Domestic Violence in Ireland: Where to Find Help, How to Report and Your Rights
violencia-domestica-irlanda-onde-encontr.en_excerpt: Where to seek help, how to contact the Garda, protective orders and immigration rights.
violencia-domestica-irlanda-onde-encontr.en_content:
If you are living with domestic violence in Ireland, you do not have to face it alone. Public services, specialist organisations, legal support, police protection and court measures are available.

Domestic violence is not only physical assault. It can also involve threats, control, sexual violence, emotional abuse, financial control, digital abuse and coercive behaviour.

If you are in danger now

If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999 or 112 and ask An Garda Síochána for help.

You can also go to your nearest Garda Station. If you do not speak English well, that should not stop you from asking for help.

What is domestic violence?

  • physical assault;
  • threats or intimidation;
  • sexual violence or coercion;
  • psychological or emotional control;
  • financial control;
  • control through technology or social media;
  • stalking or unwanted contact;
  • coercive or controlling behaviour;
  • threats against children or family members;
  • destruction of property.

The Courts Service explains that domestic violence can be carried out by current or former partners, spouses, civil partners, people with whom you have had an intimate relationship, the other parent of your children and certain family members.

Official links: Apply for a domestic violence protection order

Where to find help in Ireland?

Women’s Aid

Women’s Aid runs a free, confidential national helpline for women experiencing domestic violence.

1800 341 900 — 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

Men’s Aid

Men can also be victims of domestic violence. The HSE lists Men’s Aid among the national support services.

01 554 3811

National Male Advice Line

The HSE also lists the National Male Advice Line as a support service.

1800 816 588

HSE

The HSE holds information on domestic, sexual and gender-based violence services and lists national and local services.

Do I need to report to the Garda immediately?

If there is immediate danger, call 999 or 112. In other situations you can go to your local Garda Station to explain what happened, ask for guidance or make a report.

You can also contact specialist services before deciding whether to report. The important thing is to find a safe way to get guidance.

Official links: Report to / get help from the Garda

Make a safety plan

If it is safe to do so, consider preparing a plan for a possible emergency.

  • choose someone you trust;
  • identify a safe place where you can stay;
  • keep important documents accessible;
  • have in mind how to ask for help in an emergency;
  • if it is safe, prepare a bag with documents, keys, money, clothes and anything the children need;
  • be careful when researching help if your phone or computer is being monitored.

Do not do anything that increases your risk. If preparing documents or a bag could put you in danger, put your safety first.

Can I get a court order against the perpetrator?

Yes. Ireland has different types of Domestic Violence Orders:

  • Protection Order;
  • Safety Order;
  • Barring Order;
  • Interim Barring Order;
  • Emergency Barring Order.

Protection Order

This is a short-term protective measure. It can order the person to stop perpetrating violence or making threats. If the perpetrator lives with you, a Protection Order does not automatically order them to leave the home.

Safety Order

This is a longer-term protective order. It can prevent certain acts of violence, threats, stalking or contact. If the perpetrator lives with you, a Safety Order does not order them to leave the house. A Safety Order granted by the District Court can last up to 5 years.

Barring Order

A Barring Order can order the perpetrator to leave or not enter the home, and can impose other restrictions relating to violence, threats, stalking or contact. A Barring Order granted by the District Court can last up to 3 years.

Interim Barring Order and Emergency Barring Order

These are emergency protective measures. Whether each one can be applied for depends on the relationship between the people and on the rights to the home. The Courts Service explains the specific criteria for each order.

How do I apply for a Domestic Violence Order?

  1. Complete the Application for a Domestic Violence Order.
  2. Submit the application at the appropriate Court Office, normally the District Court.
  3. The Court Office will arrange the hearing before a judge.
  4. The Courts Service or the Gardaí will notify the respondent in line with the procedure.
  5. You may attend the full hearing so that the judge can decide on long-term protection.

If you have dependent children you want included in the protection, they must be included in the application.

The Courts Service currently provides the official Application for a Domestic Violence Order form and advises that the correct version is used before filing.

Official links: Garda - Domestic Abuse · HSE - Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence · Courts Service - Domestic Violence · Irish Immigration Service - Victims of Domestic Abuse

What if the perpetrator breaches the order?

Breaching a Domestic Violence Order is a crime. If it happens, contact the Gardaí immediately. If there is immediate danger, call 999 or 112.

What if I cannot afford a lawyer?

The Legal Aid Board provides legal advice and mediation services subject to the applicable criteria. The Government also advises victims of domestic violence to contact the Legal Aid Board for legal assistance information.

I am Brazilian. What if my immigration status is linked to my partner?

If your Irish immigration permission is linked to the partner perpetrating the violence, do not assume you have to stay in the relationship to keep your immigration status.

The Department of Justice has a procedure for victims and survivors of domestic violence whose permission is linked to the perpetrator to apply for an independent immigration permission, where the applicable criteria are met.

The Government has also announced a waiver of the immigration registration fee for people who receive this independent permission on domestic violence grounds.

Everyone’s immigration situation is different. If you hold another type of Stamp, are in an international protection process, hold European citizenship, have children or other specific circumstances, seek proper advice before making an important immigration decision.

What if I have children?

If children are involved, include their safety in your plan. Depending on the court order and the situation, dependent children can be included in the protection.

If a child is in immediate danger, call 999 or 112. You may also need advice from Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, where there are concerns about a child’s safety or welfare.

Financial and digital abuse

Domestic violence can include control over money, accounts, transport or other resources. It can also involve the use of technology to control, stalk or intimidate someone.

If you suspect your phone or computer is being monitored, be careful when researching help or installing apps. Where possible, use a secure device or ask someone you trust for help.

What to do in the next 24 hours?

  1. If there is immediate danger, call 999 or 112.
  2. If there is no immediate danger, reach out to someone you trust.
  3. Contact a specialist service.
  4. Consider making a safety plan.
  5. Seek advice about your children, housing and immigration situation.
  6. Consider speaking to the Garda.
  7. Seek legal advice if you need a court order.
  8. Do not confront the perpetrator if that could increase the risk.

Important phone numbers

Useful official links

Useful official links

  • An Garda Síochána - Domestic Abuse
  • Department of Justice - Domestic Violence
  • HSE - Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Services
  • Courts Service - Domestic Violence
  • Courts Service - Apply for a Domestic Violence Court Order
  • Courts Service - Court Forms
  • Irish Immigration Service - Victims of Domestic Abuse
  • Legal Aid Board

Official links: Check the Courts Service forms

Frequently asked questions

Can I call the Garda even if I have no evidence?

You can go to the Garda and explain what is happening. The Garda can assess the situation, investigate possible crimes and advise on protective measures and services.

Do I have to leave home before seeking help?

Not necessarily. You can seek advice and make a safety plan before deciding, as long as it is safe to do so.

Can I get a court order even if I am not divorced?

Domestic Violence Orders depend on the relationship between the people and on the applicable legal criteria. Being divorced is not a general requirement for every form of protection.

My partner is responsible for my visa. Do I have to stay with them?

Not necessarily. There are specific procedures for certain victims and survivors whose immigration permission is linked to the perpetrator to apply for an independent permission.

I am a man. Can I seek help?

Yes. There are specific male support services, including Men’s Aid and the National Male Advice Line.

I do not speak English. Can I ask for help?

Yes. When you contact the Garda, say that you need help with the language. The Garda has arrangements to make communication easier for people whose first language is not English.

One last important thing

The violence is not your fault.

You are not responsible for another person’s abusive behaviour. Nor do you have to make every decision all at once.

If you are in danger, call 999 or 112. If you are not in immediate danger, contact a specialist service and talk to someone you trust.

Last checked

Information checked: 29 August 2026.

Phone numbers, services, forms, immigration procedures, fees and criteria can change. Always confirm the details directly on the official sources before acting.

Notice: This guide is for information only and does not constitute personalised legal, immigration or safety advice. In a situation of immediate danger, call 999 or 112.
violencia-domestica-irlanda-onde-encontr.en_meta_description: Experiencing domestic violence in Ireland? See where to seek help, how to contact the Garda, protective measures and your immigration options.

inverno-irlanda-depressao-sazonal-saude-.en_title: 🌧️ Winter in Ireland and Mental Health: Seasonal Depression, Loneliness and Where to Find Help
inverno-irlanda-depressao-sazonal-saude-.en_excerpt: Recognise the signs of seasonal depression, when to seek help and which services are available in Ireland.
inverno-irlanda-depressao-sazonal-saude-.en_content:
Winter in Ireland can be challenging. The days get shorter, there is less natural light, temperatures drop and many people spend more time indoors. For anyone living far from family and home country, this period can also bring longing, loneliness and isolation.

For some people, the seasonal changes can significantly affect their mental health. This guide explains how to recognise the signs of seasonal depression, when to seek help and where to find support in Ireland.

🚨 If you are at immediate risk

If you or someone else is at immediate risk, do not wait for an online answer. Call 112 or 999 or go to a hospital Emergency Department.

The HSE also advises seeing a GP or an out-of-hours GP service when needed.

🌧️ Can winter affect our mental health?

Yes. Some people experience a type of depression linked to the changes of the seasons called Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), known in Portuguese as seasonal depression or winter depression.

According to the HSE, symptoms usually start in autumn or winter and tend to improve during spring. For some people they are mild; for others they can significantly interfere with everyday life.

Possible signs

  • persistent sadness or low mood;
  • loss of interest or pleasure in activities;
  • irritability;
  • tiredness and lack of energy;
  • anxiety or stress;
  • feelings of guilt, worthlessness or hopelessness;
  • frequent crying;
  • low self-esteem;
  • social isolation;
  • changes in sleep;
  • loss of interest in usual activities;
  • thoughts about death or suicide.

Having some of these symptoms does not automatically mean a person has SAD or depression. Persistent or significant changes in mood and behaviour deserve attention.

If symptoms of depression are present most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks, the HSE recommends talking to a GP.

🇧🇷 And for those living far from home?

For many immigrants, winter brings feelings that go beyond the weather: missing family, friends, food, sunshine and the feeling of being at home.

It is possible to love the life you have built in Ireland and still miss the life you left behind. Someone can be working, smiling and looking after everyone and still not be emotionally well.

Not all suffering is visible.

💭 “I’m fine.”

Sometimes the person who says “I’m fine” is just trying to get through the day. One simple question can make a difference: “How are you, really?”

And, most importantly: be ready to hear the answer.

🫂 How to help someone who is not well?

  • ❤️ Ask how they are.
  • ❤️ Listen without judgement.
  • ❤️ Show them they are not alone.
  • ❤️ Avoid phrases that minimise their suffering.
  • ❤️ Encourage them to seek professional help.
  • ❤️ Stay in contact, especially if they are isolating themselves.

You do not need to be a psychologist to show concern. A conversation can be the first step for someone to accept seeking help.

The HSE also advises that support services can be contacted when we are worried about someone else, not only when we are going through a personal crisis.

🚨 And when someone talks about suicide?

Take it seriously. If someone says they do not want to live any more, that they cannot take it any more, or shows suicidal thoughts, do not ignore it and do not simply try to convince them to “think positively”.

  • Listen.
  • Stay close, when it is safe to do so.
  • Encourage them to seek help.
  • Use the services available.

The HSE advises that when someone is thinking about suicide it is important to tell someone and to seek support. The person does not have to face those feelings alone.

💛 Where to get help in Ireland

📞 Samaritans

A confidential, non-judgemental emotional support service.

116 123 — available 24 hours a day, every day.

Email: jo@samaritans.ie

Samaritans Ireland - official website

Official links: 24/7 emotional support - Samaritans Ireland

💛 Pieta

Pieta supports people who are experiencing suicidal thoughts or self-harm, and people affected by someone else’s suicide.

Crisis Helpline: 1800 247 247 — 24 hours.

Text support: send HELP to 51444. The message may be charged according to your plan.

Pieta also offers therapy for people affected by suicidal thoughts, self-harm or bereavement by suicide. The service can be reached on 0818 111 126, subject to the criteria and services available.

Pieta - official website

Official links: Crisis support - Pieta

💬 Text About It

For anyone who is not comfortable talking on the phone, there is a text-based alternative.

Send HELLO to 50808.

It is a free text conversation service, available 24 hours a day, offering emotional support and help in crisis situations.

Text About It - official website

Official links: Text About It

🩺 Talk to your GP

If you notice that your mood has changed, that you are constantly without energy, have lost interest in things, are isolating yourself or feel you are not coping, talk to your GP (General Practitioner).

You do not have to wait until a crisis to seek help.

The HSE provides information on mental health services and can point you to where to find support.

HSE Mental Health Information Line

1800 111 888

This is an information line about mental health services. It does not replace an emergency service or clinical advice.

HSE - Your Mental Health Information Line

Official links: HSE information on Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) · HSE - Help for thoughts about suicide · HSE - Get urgent help for a mental health crisis · HSE - Your Mental Health Information Line

🌍 Do you not speak perfect English?

Do not let the language barrier stop you from seeking help. When contacting a health or emergency service, explain that you need help communicating and ask about the available options.

🌱 Looking after your mental health is also prevention

Prevention starts before a crisis: when we ask how someone is, we notice changes in behaviour and stop treating emotional suffering as weakness.

Seeking a GP, a psychologist or a support service does not mean someone has failed. Asking for help can be an important step in looking after yourself.

💛 You do not have to get through the winter alone

If the days are hard, reach out to someone. Talk. Ask for help. Listen to whoever needs it. Stay close to the people who make you feel looked after.

Winter passes.

You do not have to solve everything today. Sometimes it is enough to take the next step.

Talk. Listen. Hold space. Seek help.

💛 A message from Conexão BR Ireland

We are a community of Brazilians living in Ireland. And we believe that connection also means looking after one another.

If this article made you think of someone, send it to them. Maybe they need exactly this information today.

You are not alone. 🇧🇷🇮🇪💛

Sources and official information

  • HSE - Get urgent help for a mental health crisis
  • HSE - Your Mental Health Information Line
  • Samaritans Ireland
  • Pieta - Crisis Helpline

autismo-na-irlanda-diagnostico-hse-apoio.en_title: Autism in Ireland: Diagnosis, HSE and Where to Find Support
autismo-na-irlanda-diagnostico-hse-apoio.en_excerpt: How autism assessment works in Ireland for children and adults, and what support exists.
autismo-na-irlanda-diagnostico-hse-apoio.en_content:
Autism in Ireland: diagnosis, the HSE and where to find support

For Brazilians living in Ireland who are autistic — or who have a child who may be autistic — it is important to understand how the Irish health system works. The HSE provides information and different kinds of autism-related support, but the route depends on the person’s age, their needs and the services available in the area where they live.

Important: this guide is for information and does not replace a medical, psychological or individual professional assessment.

Official links: HSE information on autism assessment and support · Find HSE autism-related support · HSE - Autism

Who is this guide for?

  • autistic adults;
  • parents or carers of autistic children;
  • adults who suspect they may be autistic;
  • families moving to Ireland;
  • Brazilians who already have a diagnosis from Brazil and want to understand which supports they can seek in Ireland.

How does autism assessment work in Ireland?

The route varies by age. For children, the HSE describes different assessment and support pathways through health and disability services. For adults, the current HSE information is different: the HSE states that it does not provide adult autism diagnostic assessment, and advises anyone seeking an assessment to consider a private assessment with a psychologist.

Check the official HSE page on autism assessment before starting the process, because services, referrals and availability can change.

If the person is a child

If you believe your child may be autistic, the HSE recommends speaking to a health or education professional. Depending on the situation, the route may involve the GP, the Public Health Nurse, the Primary Care Team, the Children’s Disability Network Team (CDNT) or the school.

  • book an appointment with the GP, or speak to the health professional who already looks after the child;
  • explain which behaviours, communication needs, learning difficulties or sensory issues led you to seek help;
  • ask which local service is the right one;
  • keep relevant reports and documentation ready to show professionals.

If the child already has a diagnosis in Brazil

A diagnosis carried out in Brazil can help explain the child’s history to the professionals who will support them in Ireland. Bring diagnostic reports, school reports, therapy information and other relevant documents.

  • diagnostic report;
  • reports from psychologists, therapists or doctors;
  • school reports;
  • information about therapies carried out;
  • a list of medication, where applicable;
  • a description of communication and sensory needs.

If the documents are in Portuguese, check in advance with the service receiving them whether a translation will be required. Do not assume a certified translation is mandatory: the requirement depends on the service and the purpose of the documents.

Adults who suspect they are autistic

The HSE currently states that it does not provide adult autism diagnostic assessment. The official advice is to seek a private assessment. The HSE also points to professional organisations such as the Psychological Society of Ireland (PSI) as a reference for finding professionals.

Before booking, confirm directly with the professional what type of assessment is offered, the cost, the timeframe and which documents will be needed. HSE - adult autism assessment

Is it possible to get support without a diagnosis?

The HSE states that a person does not necessarily have to wait for a formal diagnosis to access certain services. A health professional can advise on the most suitable service for the needs presented.

This can be especially relevant for families waiting for an assessment. See HSE - where to get support and talk to the GP or another professional who supports the person.

What kinds of support may be available?

Support depends on individual needs. The HSE describes different services and professionals who may be involved, including psychologists, psychiatrists, occupational therapists, speech and language therapists, disability services and mental health services where needed.

The HSE also points to organisations such as AsIAm and the Irish Society for Autism as sources of information and support. HSE - where to get support

Benefits and social supports

Depending on the person’s and the family’s situation, different social welfare payments may exist. The HSE mentions, among others, Carer’s Allowance, Carer’s Benefit, Carer’s Support Grant, Domiciliary Care Allowance and Disability Allowance.

Being autistic does not automatically mean you are entitled to a payment. Each scheme has its own criteria. To check eligibility, contact the Department of Social Protection and Citizens Information.

Autism and education

For children, talk to the school about individual communication, learning, routine and sensory needs. For third-level education, the HSE also points to DARE as a possible support route for eligible students.

Transitioning from children’s services to adult services

The transition should be planned well in advance. The HSE recommends starting to prepare the move to adult services at around 14 or 15 years old where possible. More recent HSE information also indicates that, in some disability services, the transition can begin about 18 months before the young person leaves school.

See HSE - changing from child to adult care and HSE - moving from child to adult services.

Organisations that can help

  • HSE - Autism — official health information.
  • AsIAm — an Irish organisation dedicated to autism.
  • Irish Society for Autism — autism-related information and resources.
  • Citizens Information — information on public services and benefits.
  • Department of Social Protection — social welfare payments and social protection.

Frequently asked questions

I have an autism diagnosis from Brazil. Do I need another diagnosis in Ireland?

It is not possible to say that every Brazilian diagnosis will have to be repeated. The need depends on the service and the purpose. Bring your reports and confirm directly with the Irish service which documents are needed.

Can adults be assessed by the HSE?

The HSE currently states that it does not provide adult autism diagnostic assessment, and advises seeking a private assessment.

My child is waiting for an assessment. Can they get any support?

The HSE states that certain services can be accessed without waiting for a formal diagnosis, depending on needs. Talk to the GP or another professional to identify the right route.

Does a diagnosis automatically give entitlement to a social welfare payment?

No. Each payment has its own criteria and must be assessed individually.

Last checked

Information checked: 19 August 2026. We recommend checking the official pages before making decisions, as service availability, criteria, procedures and contacts can change.

Notice: this guide is for information only. It does not constitute personalised medical, legal, financial or professional advice.
