autismo-viagem-aviao-irlanda-dublin-cork.en_title: Autism and Air Travel in Ireland: Dublin and Cork Airport
autismo-viagem-aviao-irlanda-dublin-cork.en_excerpt: Important Flyer, Sunflower, sensory rooms and what to do if you lose the card.
autismo-viagem-aviao-irlanda-dublin-cork.en_content:
Autism and air travel in Ireland: a guide for Dublin and Cork Airport

Flying can be particularly challenging for some autistic people because of queues, noise, lighting, changes of routine, security, waiting, communication and unfamiliar environments.

Dublin Airport and Cork Airport offer specific resources for passengers with autism and other non-visible disabilities, and some airlines also have preparation programmes and materials.

Important: airport and airline services, requirements and procedures can change. Always confirm the information directly with the airport and the airline before each trip.

Official links: Accessibility/autism at Dublin Airport · Autism support at Cork Airport

Who is this guide for?

  • autistic adults;
  • parents of autistic children;
  • Brazilians travelling between Ireland and Brazil;
  • families who have never flown with an autistic person;
  • passengers with other non-visible disabilities;
  • people who may need more time or a different way of communicating during the journey.

First of all: tell the airline

One of the most important recommendations is to contact the airline before the trip. Aer Lingus has a specific area for needs relating to autism and provides an assistance request form.

If the flight is not operated by Aer Lingus, do not assume the same services will be available. Check directly with the airline operating the flight.

Prepare the person before the trip

Making the process predictable can help. Cork Airport recommends preparing the person well in advance using visual resources, photographs and explanations of each step of the journey.

  1. leaving home;
  2. arriving at the airport;
  3. checking in;
  4. handing over the bag;
  5. going through security;
  6. finding the gate;
  7. waiting;
  8. boarding;
  9. sitting on the plane;
  10. taking off;
  11. arriving at the destination;
  12. leaving the airport.

Visit the airport before the trip

If possible, getting to know the airport before the day of the flight can help. Cork Airport recommends a prior visit to familiarise the person with the environment, including the movement and the noise.

Use visual resources

Photographs and symbols can help explain what will happen. Cork Airport recommends visual guides for situations such as check-in, security, queues, the gate, boarding and waiting. Aer Lingus also offers visual guides for the different stages of the journey.

Important Flyer — Dublin Airport

Dublin Airport has a programme called Important Flyer for passengers with autism or a Sensory Processing Disorder. The identifier can be a lanyard or a wristband, and it discreetly signals to staff that the passenger may need more time, clear communication, a calmer environment or additional understanding.

How to apply

  1. complete the Important Flyer form;
  2. attach a one-page letter from a GP or an AsIAm card confirming an autism or SPD diagnosis;
  3. make a separate application for each person who needs the identifier;
  4. provide the Eircode.

Dublin Airport states that Important Flyer delivery is available to postal addresses in Ireland, including Northern Ireland, and that there is currently no airport collection option.

Important Flyer and Fast Track

Dublin Airport states that Fast Track must be booked in advance. Up to four Fast Track passes can be free when the programme conditions are met. The Important Flyer holder must be travelling; the airport states that up to three companions may travel with the holder using this benefit on the same day.

Do not confuse: having an autism card is not the same as taking part in the Important Flyer programme. You have to follow the airport’s procedure and make the booking where it applies.

Sunflower at Dublin Airport

Dublin Airport takes part in the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower scheme. The airport states that its staff are trained to recognise the symbol and to offer additional support, understanding or more time when needed. The airport advises passengers to use the PRM Assist App to request Sunflower use.

Hidden Disabilities Sunflower keeps an international list of participating airports, but the kind of support varies by airport.

Official links: Dublin Airport - Autism & non-visible disabilities

Sensory room at Dublin Airport

Dublin Airport - Sensory Room has Sensory Rooms in both terminals for passengers who may become overwhelmed by the airport environment.

  • the sessions are free;
  • each session lasts 60 minutes;
  • there is no walk-in service;
  • the rooms are after security;
  • there is one room in Terminal 1, near the Gates 200;
  • there is one room in Terminal 2, near the Gates 400.

The room must be booked in advance. If you have already booked assistance, an OCS agent can help during security and accompany the passenger to the room and then to the gate.

Cork Airport: Sunflower Lanyard

Cork Airport - Autism / ASD offers support for passengers with non-visible disabilities. The airport states that passengers with autism can use a Sunflower Lanyard, available free of charge at the OCS desk in the terminal.

Official links: Cork Airport - Autism/ASD support

Cork Airport: Sensory Pod

Cork Airport has a sensory pod for passengers with non-visible disabilities. The space is free, must be booked, and it is recommended to request it in advance; the airport recommends around 48 hours where possible.

Assistance to move through the airport

If the person needs help to move through the airport, request assistance in advance. At Cork Airport the service can help from arrival at the airport to boarding. The airport recommends booking through the airline or the responsible agent, because asking for assistance only on arrival can mean waiting.

Identification and assistance are not necessarily the same thing. A Sunflower lanyard does not replace an assistance booking.

Official links: Request special assistance with Aer Lingus

Autism ID cards

There are different identification cards available in Ireland and they are not equivalent.

AsIAm Autism ID Card

AsIAm offers an Autism ID Card. The organisation currently states a cost of €27.50, inclusion of a lanyard and holder, processing of up to eight weeks, validity of three years for children and five years for adults, plus formal proof of diagnosis and a photograph.

AsIAm itself explains that the card serves as proof of diagnosis and can be shown to service providers, but it does not automatically guarantee discounts, preferential treatment or benefits. Any support depends on the service used.

ASD Ireland ID Card

ASD Ireland also has its own card. The organisation currently states a cost of €20 and validity of two years, and requires clinical documentation proving the diagnosis.

This card is an ASD Ireland programme of its own and should not be confused with the AsIAm card or the Dublin Airport Important Flyer.

What to put in the bag?

  • headphones;
  • ear defenders;
  • a toy or regulating object;
  • a tablet or entertainment device;
  • a charger or power bank, where allowed;
  • suitable food;
  • any medication needed;
  • documents;
  • identification cards;
  • visual resources;
  • contact details.

And medication?

If the person takes medication or has specific dietary needs, check the rules of the airline, the airport and the destination country well in advance. Cork Airport states that, in certain situations, a letter from a GP can help explain needs related to medication or diet during the trip.

This does not replace airport security rules or immigration/customs rules.

And if there is a meltdown or sensory overload?

  1. move to a quieter place;
  2. reduce stimuli;
  3. use headphones or another familiar resource;
  4. use simple communication;
  5. offer a break;
  6. avoid too many questions;
  7. follow the visual plan;
  8. tell the airport team if assistance is needed.

There is no universal strategy for every autistic person. Cork Airport emphasises that each person understands and experiences social situations differently and that strategies must be adapted to the individual.

Checklist before leaving home

2–3 weeks before

  • confirm the flight;
  • confirm the assistance services;
  • contact the airline;
  • check the options available at the airport;
  • prepare visual resources;
  • practise the travel sequence;
  • check documents;
  • prepare medication and medical information;
  • book the Sensory Room, where available;
  • request the Important Flyer, if applicable;
  • arrange the Sunflower or another identifier.

A few days before

  • confirm times;
  • check the baggage rules again;
  • charge devices;
  • prepare the bag;
  • print important documents;
  • review the visual plan.

On the day of travel

  • arrive with enough time;
  • tell the team if you need assistance;
  • keep comfort resources accessible;
  • follow the visual sequence;
  • allow time for breaks;
  • have a plan for delays.

Note: services can change

Accessibility programmes, availability of rooms, assistance procedures and Fast Track conditions can change. Always confirm directly with the airport, the airline or the responsible organisation before the trip.

Useful links

Useful links

  • Dublin Airport - Autism & Non-Visible Disabilities
  • Dublin Airport - Sensory Room
  • Cork Airport - Travelling With Autism
  • Aer Lingus - Needs Relating to Autism
  • AsIAm - Autism ID Card
  • ASD Ireland - ID Card
  • Hidden Disabilities Sunflower - Airports Around the World

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an autism card to travel?

Not necessarily. The cards are a form of identification or proof, but the assistance procedures depend on the airport and the airline.

Does the AsIAm Autism ID Card guarantee Fast Track?

No. The AsIAm card and the Dublin Airport Important Flyer are different things. The free Fast Track described by Dublin Airport is tied to the Important Flyer programme and requires advance booking.

Can I use the Sunflower at the airport?

Dublin Airport takes part in the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower network and states that its staff are trained to recognise the symbol. Cork Airport also provides Sunflower lanyards.

Is the Dublin Airport sensory room free?

Yes. The airport states that the sessions are free, last 60 minutes and must be booked in advance. There are no walk-ins.

Can I just arrive at the airport and ask for assistance?

It is better not to rely on that. Cork Airport recommends booking assistance in advance because there may be a wait if the request is only made on arrival.

Does the airline need to know I am travelling with an autistic person?

It is highly recommended to tell the airline in advance and ask which assistance services are available. Aer Lingus has a specific procedure for needs relating to autism.

Does the Sunflower work in other countries?

The Hidden Disabilities Sunflower network is international and includes many airports, but the kind of support offered varies. Always check the specific airport before travelling.

Last checked

Information checked: 19 August 2026. Card prices, booking rules, room availability, assistance procedures and Fast Track conditions can change. Always confirm directly with the airport, the airline or the responsible organisation before the trip.

Notice: this guide is for information and does not constitute personalised medical, legal or travel advice.

Who we are

Conexão BR Irlanda is the portal of the Brazilian community in Ireland. Our goal is to connect, inform and support Brazilians who live in Ireland or plan to move here.

Our Mission

To provide relevant information, practical guides, events and a support network so that every Brazilian can live better in Ireland.

Our Vision

To be the main reference for the Brazilian community in Ireland, promoting integration, knowledge and opportunities.

Our Values

  • Community and solidarity
  • Quality, verified information
  • Inclusion and diversity
  • Transparency and trust

outono-irlanda-alimentacao-bem-estar.en_title: Autumn has arrived in Ireland… and so has the change in our bodies
outono-irlanda-alimentacao-bem-estar.en_excerpt: For Brazilians living in Ireland, autumn brings shorter days and changes to your routine. Here are simple ideas for adapting your diet, staying hydrated and looking after your wellbeing through the colder months.
outono-irlanda-alimentacao-bem-estar.en_content:
For us Brazilians who live in Ireland, the arrival of autumn can be a real change.

Days start getting shorter, we have fewer hours of daylight, temperatures drop, and little by little our routine changes too. We start to notice differences in our energy, our mood, our appetite, and even that urge to get out of the house and move around.

Autumn changes our routine

And our diet follows that change too.

Perhaps that salad that tasted so good in summer is not quite as appealing now. The chilled smoothie loses its appeal and we start looking for warmer, more comforting food.

And that is perfectly fine. 💚

A healthy diet does not have to look the same all year round. We can adapt our choices to the seasons, respecting our preferences while keeping a balanced and nutritious way of eating.

Adapting your diet to autumn

🍲 Not in the mood for salad?

You do not have to force yourself. Soups, stews, roasted vegetables, sautéed or grilled vegetables are all great ways to keep getting vegetables into your meals.

🍎 What about fruit?

Fruit can be given a cosier treatment too. Try baking apples or pears with cinnamon, stewing fruit, or adding fruit to dishes such as banana pancakes, warm overnight oats, or a homemade apple cake.

💧 Have you noticed you are drinking less water?

That can happen when the cold sets in. Keep your bottle close by and take the opportunity to add sugar-free teas and infusions throughout the day. They can contribute to your hydration too.

🥣 Use warm dishes to widen your variety

Soups and the famous Irish stews are a great opportunity to include different vegetables, beans, lentils, chickpeas and other pulses. Warm, comforting food can be nutritious as well.

Adapt, do not fight the season

And that may be one of the most important things to remember at this time of year: we do not have to fight against the season.

We can adapt our diet, our routine and our habits to what this time of year is asking of us, without giving up on looking after our health.

Autumn Survival Guide for Ireland 🍂

That is why I have put together an Autumn Survival Guide for Ireland 🍂, with practical tips to help you get through the colder months while looking after your diet and your wellbeing. I will leave the guide here for you all. 💚

One-to-one support

And if you feel you need more individualised support — whether for weight loss and weight management, high cholesterol, pre-diabetes, improving your relationship with food, or simply building healthier habits that really work in your routine here in Ireland — send me a message.

It would be a pleasure to work with you. 🌿

carne-refogada-ao-estilo-korean-bbq.en_excerpt: By: Chef Anderson Balico, Food Content Creator & Digital Marketing.
carne-refogada-ao-estilo-korean-bbq.en_content:
By: Chef Anderson Balico, Food Content Creator & Digital Marketing

Ingredients

400 g of strips of beef

2 tablespoons of Korean BBQ ÍON Organic Seasoning

2 tablespoons of soy sauce (shoyu)

1 tablespoon of honey

1 tablespoon of ÍON sunflower oil

1 red pepper, sliced

1 onion, sliced

1 spring onion, finely chopped

Method:

Coat the beef with the soy sauce, honey and Korean BBQ seasoning. Leave to marinate for 15 minutes.

Heat the sunflower oil in a very hot frying pan or wok and stir-fry the beef for about 5 minutes, until golden.

Add the onion and red pepper and cook for a further 3 to 4 minutes, until tender.

Finish with the spring onion and serve with rice or pasta.

sol-e-lua-equilibrando-consciencia-e-emo.en_title: Sun and Moon: Balancing Consciousness and Emotions Through the Northern European Winter
sol-e-lua-equilibrando-consciencia-e-emo.en_excerpt: The Sun and the Moon play a fascinating role in our lives, influencing both our consciousness and our emotions. Practical tips for facing the northern European winter.
sol-e-lua-equilibrando-consciencia-e-emo.en_content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

The Sun and the Moon play a fascinating role in our lives, influencing both our consciousness and our emotions.

The Sun, with its majestic presence, is our central star, providing the vital energy that keeps us alive. It symbolises consciousness, self-assertion and the capacity to express our own light into the world. When we think of the Sun, we can imagine the strength and confidence it inspires in us, like a powerful and just lion.

The Moon, on the other hand, is the queen of emotions and emotional intelligence. She reflects the light of the Sun and is intimately connected to our most sensitive side. The Moon influences not only the tides and nature, but also our feelings, intuitions and memories. Each lunar phase affects us in its own way, from the introspection of the new moon to the intensity of the full moon.

During the winter in northern Europe, when the days are short and the nights long, keeping a mental and emotional balance can be challenging. Here are a few practical tips to help you face this season:

  • Get out in natural light whenever you can: make the most of the sunny moments to help regulate your body clock and improve your mood.

  • Exercise regularly: exercise does not only warm the body, it also releases endorphins, which are essential for mental wellbeing.

  • Keep a routine: fixed times for waking, eating and sleeping help maintain emotional stability.

  • Cultivate moments of self-care: meditation, relaxing reading or a warm bath can help calm the mind and nurture the emotions.

  • Stay connected with other people: even when the weather invites you to withdraw, keeping in touch with friends and family is crucial for emotional support.

It is worth noticing that many cultures around the world have different interpretations of the influence of the Sun and the Moon on our lives. Some see the Sun as a symbol of authority and leadership, while others associate it with a spiritual guide. In the same way, the Moon, in its constant change, is seen as a magical and seductive force inviting us to reflect and to connect with our inner self.

Would you like to know more about how these celestial forces can influence your daily life? Leave a comment and I will bring more information in the next article.

Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

o-inverno-do-ego-um-renascimento-poetico.en_title: The Winter of the Ego — A Poetic Rebirth
o-inverno-do-ego-um-renascimento-poetico.en_excerpt: There is a season inside every soul in which everything grows quieter: a gentle inner winter where the Ego loosens its grip and everything in excess begins to fall away.
o-inverno-do-ego-um-renascimento-poetico.en_content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

There is a season inside every soul in which everything grows quieter.

A gentle inner winter, in which the Ego loosens its grip and everything in excess begins to fall away.

Winter is not a punishment — it is preparation.

It strips us gently, like the trees letting go of their leaves, to reveal what is

true beneath the noise: the procrastination, the fear, the resistance, the unconscious

search for validation.

Everything that limits our capacity to give, to grow and to serve.

This is the sacred process of deconstructing the Ego — the cleaning of the inner soil.

When we surrender, even in silence, we launch our intention to the Universe.

Not out of the Ego’s need to receive, but out of the soul’s readiness to grow.

True spirituality begins here: in honesty, in service, in the willingness to let old identities dissolve.

Winter teaches us our limits and our desires, what no longer belongs, and what still

pulses to stay.

And then, without effort, Spring arrives.

Spring is born when the Ego softens, when the inner ground thaws just enough for new seeds to put down roots.

All at once clarity becomes action, love becomes presence, and the act of giving becomes the natural language of the heart.

There is no blossoming without its Winter.

You cannot sow into frozen ground.

You have to allow yourself to be taken apart first.

This is the rhythm of healing:

Winter cleanses.

Spring is reborn.

And the soul, patient and luminous, crosses the bridge between the two.

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist
o-inverno-do-ego-um-renascimento-poetico.en_meta_description: There is a season inside every soul in which everything grows quieter. Winter is not a punishment — it is preparation.

o-sol-que-habita-em-nos.en_title: The Sun That Lives in Us
o-sol-que-habita-em-nos.en_excerpt: December arrives as a warm embrace in the middle of the cold. Missing home can be a bridge, not just a weight.
o-sol-que-habita-em-nos.en_content:
Text: Ana Luiza A Duarte

Integrative Therapist

December arrives as a warm embrace in the middle of the cold.

While the streets light up and the world seems to adorn itself with promises, there are those who feel a sweet longing — for home, for family, for the language, for the smell of fresh coffee coming from the kitchen. It is the heart trying to find its place even far from where it began. It is natural to miss the sun that accompanied us all year long. To miss the light that warmed the skin, the full table, the familiar voices. But perhaps it is now, in the middle of this foreign winter, that we can rediscover another kind of warmth — the kind that is born from meeting, from sharing, from presence.

Missing home can be a bridge. It can take us to the other, to the new community that welcomes us, to the affinities that bring us together. An invitation to open the doors of the house and of the heart, to build bonds that warm us when the sun is slow to appear.

And while the year says goodbye, something in us is also reorganising itself. The silence between one celebration and the next invites us to look inwards: what do we want to carry forward? What do we leave to bloom again in 2025?

There is always a spark that holds on, even on the shortest days.

Perhaps the secret is to remember that the light we seek so much on the outside also lives

inside us.

That the summer warmth left behind can be rekindled in the smile of a new friend,

in a gesture of care, in a moment of gratitude.

So this December, light your own sun.

Gather. Share. Celebrate — even from a distance.

Because when we meet, home happens again — wherever we are.

Ana Luiza A Duarte

Integrative Therapist
o-sol-que-habita-em-nos.en_meta_description: December arrives as a warm embrace in the middle of the cold — and missing home can become a bridge to a new community.

o-calor-que-nasce-do-inverno.en_title: The Warmth That Is Born of Winter
o-calor-que-nasce-do-inverno.en_excerpt: Winter arrives with its dense air, its short days and an unavoidable inwardness — and while the world seems to fall asleep, something in us begins to wake.
o-calor-que-nasce-do-inverno.en_content:
Text: Ana Luiza A Duarte

Integrative Therapist

Winter arrives with its dense air, its short days and a certain unavoidable withdrawal. And while the world seems to fall asleep, something in us begins to awaken. It is time to listen to what the body is asking for, what the heart whispers, what the soul wants to keep.

Cold, sometimes, is a form of care: it slows us down, preserves, protects what is yet to bloom. And since it is time to preserve and prepare, perhaps winter is also an invitation to choose.

Before sowing the seeds, you have to know what you want to see grow. Which dreams deserve to germinate when the sun warms the earth again? Which ideas, feelings or plans do you

want to nurture now, in the silence, so that they sprout with strength when the season turns?

Because inner warmth is not limited to the body — it can take the form of ideas that catch light, of intentions that warm, of plans that take shape even in the cold.

They are small embers that keep alive the hope of a new blossoming.

While everything outside seems quiet, inside us something reorganises itself. What looks like a pause is, in fact, preparation. Rest is the fertile ground for everything that is to come.

There is a kind of warmth that does not come from fire — it is born slowly, in silence, when the cold invites us to turn inwards.

It is a warmth that springs from the heart and needs to be nurtured with care. The mind, fed by prosperous thoughts, by inspiring ideas and by gestures that awaken creativity, helps keep that flame lit. This warmth heals us, wakes us, and allows us to give new ideas their first flight — small sparks that can bring us closer to ourselves and to the people around us.

Perhaps it is exactly this withdrawal that lets us reach our creative source.

To create, we have to become sensitive to what surrounds us, notice the possibilities around us, choose what inspires us and turn it into something unique — an action, an expression, an idea carrying passion and determination. When the noise outside diminishes, we manage to hear those subtle voices within us, the ones asking for space, form and colour.

Winter, with its calm, creates the perfect ground for imagining and recreating what we want to live.

So, light your little fires: a book, a song, a hot soup, a good memory. Allow yourself that warmth born from within, spreading slowly.

Winter is a reminder that true warmth is not only in the sun — it is in what we choose to nurture when the world grows cold.

Ana Luiza A Duarte

Integrative Therapist
o-calor-que-nasce-do-inverno.en_meta_description: Winter is an invitation to choose. A warmth that is born inside us is the one that heals us and gives new ideas their first flight.

preparando-o-corpo-para-o-inverno.en_excerpt: The role of food, rest and grounding in the autumn transition. Written by Simone Holz, Holistic Nutritional Therapist.
preparando-o-corpo-para-o-inverno.en_content:
The role of food, rest and grounding in the autumn transition.

Text: Simone Holz

Holistic Nutritional Therapist

Autumn is the season in which the mornings begin to turn colder, the sun says goodbye earlier and nature silently shifts its rhythm. The trees let go of what no longer serves them, and that same movement invites us to introspect, to turn inwards, to nourish the roots and to prepare body, mind and soul for the stillness of the winter to come.

Just as the earth reorganises itself, our body enters this same process of adaptation. In the first weeks of autumn it is common to feel heavier, with muscles and joints more sensitive, a tiredness that arrives without warning, or a deeper sleep that asks for more time at rest. All of this is natural: the

organism is detoxifying the excess heat, sugar and stimulation of summer — the ice creams, the long days, the accelerated pace.

Autumn is nature’s gentle reminder that it is time to slow down, clear what has accumulated and strengthen our foundations. It is the time to “put down roots” and let go of what has already done its job,

be it toxins, emotions or habits that no longer sustain our vitality.

Through autumn our body begins to ask for more nourishing, denser and warmer foods, and it is not by chance. This is the moment when we need to strengthen our immune

system and build energy reserves for winter.

This is the phase of nourishing and fortifying. Nature already offers us exactly what we need: earth foods,

root vegetables — potato, carrot, beetroot, turnip, parsnip. These are naturally richer in complex carbohydrates and minerals, providing steady energy and supporting inner warmth. It is as if the earth itself were saying: “the time to root has come.”

In Irish culture, this ancestral wisdom is reflected in the stews, coddle and typical soups of the season — warm, comforting dishes that combine root vegetables,

legumes and herbs: a simple and delicious way to warm the body and strengthen immunity.

Beyond that, this is the moment to look with care at the nutrients that sustain our natural defences. Vitamin C, present in citrus fruits, kiwi and peppers,

helps protect the cells; zinc, found in pumpkin seeds and nuts, is essential for immune function; and selenium, present in eggs and Brazil

nuts, plays a fundamental role in thyroid hormone regulation and antioxidant protection. Vitamin D, often reduced by lower

sun exposure, can be reinforced through foods such as oily fish (salmon, sardines) and eggs, or with professional guidance on supplementation. Small adjustments to what you eat make a big difference to the body’s ability to face the cold with balance and vitality.

Another essential point is caring for the gut microbiota, the basis of our immune system. Including fermented foods such as sauerkraut, kefir, kombucha or natural yoghurt helps keep the gut healthy and the body more resistant to infection. Good fats such as olive oil, avocado, seeds and nuts nourish the cells, support hormonal balance and favour the production of serotonin and melatonin — neurotransmitters linked to mood and sleep, which tend to fluctuate at this time of year. This nutritional transition, at once simple and wise, stabilises blood sugar, calms the nervous system and prepares the body for winter’s retreat with strength and serenity.

Autumn is an invitation to pause, a space between doing and being, between the movement of summer and the withdrawal of winter. It is the moment to quieten a little of the outside noise and listen to the body, which wisely shows what it needs: more rest, more warmth, more presence. Preparing for winter is not only about reinforcing

immunity, but about cultivating an inner state of balance and welcome.

Every nourishing meal, every well-slept night, every conscious breath is an act of love and respect for the body that sustains you. When you allow yourself to slow down and nourish your roots now, you create the fertile ground for crossing the cold months with energy, clarity and serenity.

This autumn, listen to your body. Slow the pace down, warm your soul and trust the natural process of the seasons.

When you align with the cycle of nature, you discover that winter is not the end — it is the rest needed for the blossoming that is to come.

Simone Holz

Holistic Nutritional Therapist

movimento-e-medicina.en_excerpt: Text: Ana Paula, Personal Trainer https://www.instagram.com/fitandstrongwithana/ — building training routines you can actually keep, for life.
movimento-e-medicina.en_content:
Text: Ana Paula, Personal Trainer

https://www.instagram.com/fitandstrongwithana/

As a woman over 30, I understand the difficulty of fitting a training routine into everyday life. I also know how essential it is, because from that age on we begin to lose muscle mass at an accelerated rate, which directly affects bone density. Strength training is the best tool for counteracting that process, and that is why I insist so much on building routines my clients can genuinely maintain in the long term — for life.

As a Personal Trainer, my mission is to help each client find the best exercise routine, aligned with their reality and their lifestyle, so that training is continuous and sustainable rather than momentary. After all, physical exercise is a lifelong commitment, not merely a means of achieving the “summer body”.

My name is Ana Paula and I have been a Personal Trainer for 5 years. I am passionate about movement and about helping people — beginners especially — take that first step into an exercise routine, promoting a better relationship with exercise and with food as well.

Over those five years I have also taken professional courses in Nutrition and Mat Pilates, because I believe constant updating is fundamental. To genuinely contribute to improving physical health — which is directly linked to mental health — it is essential to keep learning continuously and, above all, to listen to each client, respecting their story and their experiences.

Movement is medicine!

To age with health, autonomy and quality of life, we need to stay strong.

dois-anos-novos-um-medido-pelo-homem-out.en_title: Two New Years: One Measured by Man, the Other Felt by the Earth
dois-anos-novos-um-medido-pelo-homem-out.en_excerpt: The Gregorian calendar organises society; the solar return rules energy. Living inside both cycles means learning to speak two languages.
dois-anos-novos-um-medido-pelo-homem-out.en_content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

Once upon a time — not in the sky, but on paper — human beings decided where the year should begin.

The Gregorian calendar was created to organise society, not consciousness. Dated 1582, it was instituted by Pope Gregory. It aligns contracts, taxes, harvests, work, debts and systems of governance. Time became something that could be counted,

regulated, inspected and controlled. The reason was: for civilisation to work at scale, a common agreement was needed — and so 1 January was chosen as the starting line: clean, numeric, administrative.

This calendar governs the material agreement of life: bills, deadlines, fiscal years, the school calendar, productivity targets. It belongs to the constructed dimension of reality, where continuity, control and predictability are essential. It does not answer to nature — it organises people.

And that is not a flaw. It is its function. And nothing beyond that.

But, in parallel with that created rhythm, there is another year — one that does not begin by decision, but by alignment.

The solar return, in energetic and astrological terms, happens when the Sun enters Aries. That moment marks the true beginning of the solar cycle. It is when the light starts to overcome the darkness, when the Earth tilts again towards growth, when life receives the signal to move forward. This is not symbolic; it is seasonal, biological, energetic.

Aries inaugurates movement. The seeds awaken. The blood warms. The systems come online. Long before calendars existed, life on Earth was already responding to this change. That is why many ancient cultures recognised spring — and not midwinter — as the true New Year.

The solar return governs energy, not administration.

It rules vitality, instinct, initiative, courage and birth.

It belongs to nature, to astrology, to the time lived in the body.

So we live inside two simultaneous cycles, two dimensions of existence, two

timelines.

One begins in January and asks:

How are you going to manage your life?

How will you pay, plan, organise, keep going?

The other begins when the Sun enters Aries and asks:

How are you going to live it?

What do you want to be born, to be initiated, to incarnate?

Winter — January, February and much of March in the northern hemisphere — exists between these two thresholds. By the Gregorian calendar it looks like a beginning. By the solar calendar it is still an ending.

That is why so many people feel discomfort in early January.

The system says “move forward”.

The body answers “not yet”.

Winter is the last chapter of the energetic year. It is the phase of fertile decomposition. The nervous system slows down. The psyche reviews. The body conserves. Expecting full performance in this period is not discipline — it is misalignment.

Caring for yourself while respecting both systems is learning to speak two languages.

● Mind: use January to organise, not to launch. Plan without demanding immediate execution. Structure without pressure.

● Body: honour the low energy as functional, not as failure. Sleep more. Eat more densely. Move gently.

● Emotions: allow the introspection. Winter brings truths to the surface so they do not sabotage spring. Emotions are information, not obstacles.

So, when the Sun enters Aries, something changes naturally. Action stops being forced.

Decisions gain warmth. The direction becomes clear.

The Gregorian calendar keeps society running.

The solar return keeps you alive.

When both are honoured, life stops looking like resistance — and becomes rhythm instead.
dois-anos-novos-um-medido-pelo-homem-out.en_meta_description: The Gregorian calendar organises society, but the solar return rules energy. How to honour both cycles in January.

coragem-a-estrela-que-ilumina-o-caminho-.en_title: Courage! The Star That Lights the Entrepreneur’s Path — Christmas Special
coragem-a-estrela-que-ilumina-o-caminho-.en_excerpt: By Sonia Campos, MSc in Information Science and Specialist in Business Intelligence. Being an entrepreneur is, above all, an act of faith.
coragem-a-estrela-que-ilumina-o-caminho-.en_content:
The end of the year always invites us to reflect.

The Christmas lights do not only light up the streets of our cities, but also that which we so often let go out along the entrepreneurial journey: the flame of courage.

Being an entrepreneur is, above all, an act of faith. Faith in an idea, faith in a purpose, faith in your own ability to get up after every stumble. Because stumbles will come, and they are not a sign of weakness.

They are part of the route. In fact, nobody builds something extraordinary by walking in a straight line. The great business stories are born precisely in the detours, in the route adjustments, in the ability to stop, breathe deeply and decide to try again. And here is a truth that few will tell you. Money is not enough.

An academic qualification is not enough. Having done every course, gone through every mentorship and studied hard is not enough. Those elements help a great deal, but they do not sustain a business on their own. The backbone of entrepreneurship, yesterday, today and always, is courage! Courage to start. Courage to take the calculated risks and the uncalculated ones. Courage to recalculate the route a thousand times, if necessary.

Courage to keep going even when nobody understands what you see. While some believe that entrepreneurship is about strategy, others think it is about capital. But we know: entrepreneurship is about heart. About putting your soul into every attempt and understanding that growing is not a destination, it is a continuous movement.

This Christmas, allow yourself to celebrate not only the results, but above all the journey. Celebrate the attempts, the falls, the restarts. Celebrate every time you dared to believe, even when everything seemed uncertain.

And may the coming year bring new routes, new ideas, new possibilities and the courage to travel them. Happy Christmas!

May this date renew your strength, your faith and your determination to keep creating, daring and building.
coragem-a-estrela-que-ilumina-o-caminho-.en_meta_description: Money and qualifications are not enough to sustain a business. Courage is the backbone of entrepreneurship, today and always.

1-cuidando-de-si-em-terra-estrangeira.en_title: 1. Caring for Yourself in a Foreign Land
1-cuidando-de-si-em-terra-estrangeira.en_excerpt: Text: Lili Fraga, Therapist and Parenting Educator. Central theme: self-care as an adaptation tool in immigration.
1-cuidando-de-si-em-terra-estrangeira.en_content:
Text: Lili Fraga

Therapist and Parenting Educator

Central theme: self-care as an adaptation tool in immigration

Emotional difficulties, overload, missing family and the feeling of always being in survival mode. How do you create moments of pause, connection with yourself and simple practices to protect your mental health even with little time or few resources?

✨ Caring for Yourself in a Foreign Land

A look at the emotional wellbeing of those who start again outside Brazil

Living far from your country of origin can be challenging. On top of the demands of everyday life, the immigrant faces deep emotional layers — often marked by a sense of not belonging. Some discover an incredible resilience and recognise their inner strength. Others decide to return to their country. And some take on the challenge of finding a new place in the world. What we know is that we Brazilians — with our warm blood, easy laughter and exposed affections — carry far more than other people’s eyes can see.

The truth is that there is no single path to happiness and wellbeing. Being well far from home invites us on a journey of self-knowledge, in which we learn to respect our limits, to accept that we will not always be understood and that we may not be able to please everyone. Sometimes we need to create our own space in order to feel at ease with the discomfort.

And that is not only poetry. Studies show that self-care practices (such as building routines, maintaining social ties or spirituality) are fundamental to the mental health of immigrants and refugees, with psychological and social strategies proving the most effective in preventing anxiety, sadness and chronic discouragement (Mehjabeen et al., 2023). In addition, public health researchers in Ireland warn about the importance of access to culturally sensitive services that respect our language, our history and our time of adaptation (McMahon et al., 2021).

Looking after our own wellbeing is necessary. Creating relationships that allow us to be who we really are is crucial to crossing this path of beginnings, where emotional bridges may look fragile but can be built with affection and courage.

And that is why I invite you to look at one moment at a time, to make your choices based on your reality and to live at peace with yourself. You will notice that happiness can indeed be part of your nomadic life — not as a fixed destination, but as a state of presence.

If you need help, do not hesitate to ask for it. Far from home, we can build a new home — as long as we are aware of the pillars that support it.

🗓️ Next month we will talk about: “Mental Health and Immigration – What Nobody Tells You”. We will make space to talk about anxiety, insomnia, guilt, and what to do when it feels like you are losing your strength.

I will be waiting for you there. With care, Lili Fraga — Therapist and Parenting Educator www.instagram.com/lilifraga.vivaleve

2-saude-mental-e-imigracao-o-que-ninguem.en_title: 2. Mental Health and Immigration: What Nobody Tells You
2-saude-mental-e-imigracao-o-que-ninguem.en_excerpt: Text: Lili Fraga — Therapist and Parenting Educator. Central theme: anxiety, loneliness and depression among immigrants.
2-saude-mental-e-imigracao-o-que-ninguem.en_content:
Text: Lili Fraga —

Therapist and Parenting Educator

Central theme: anxiety, loneliness and depression among immigrants

Talking about the emotional impact of starting over in another country, the pressure to make it work, and how to seek help (in Portuguese or English) in Ireland. Including warning signs and pathways to support.

🧠 Mental Health and Immigration: What Nobody Tells You

Anxiety, loneliness and depression far from home

Have you ever heard that phrase — “Just come!” — when someone talks about living abroad, doing an exchange or moving country? Well… it sounds like a light invitation, full of promises — freedom, opportunities, money, quality of life. But what almost nobody tells you is that along with the suitcases come the doubts, the pressures, the longing and, often, the emotional silence.

Sometimes the desire to change is so intense that we leave without investigating our inner resources in any depth. There is no time (or courage) to ask ourselves: “Am I ready for this new beginning?” Because yes, living abroad is a transformative experience — but it demands an enormous emotional maturity.

The worries are not limited to housing or work. They invade sleep, mood and vital energy. Starting over, reinventing yourself and, above all, finding yourself are the cornerstones that keep you from losing yourself along the way.

Living abroad demands emotional planning and deep listening:

● What are my limits?

● How do I deal with frustration?

● Am I willing to live the new without erasing who I am?

And that is where the central point of this conversation comes in: mental health in immigration.

🔍 The psychological impact of starting over

Studies point to immigrants having higher rates of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress than local populations. This happens for several reasons: social isolation, language difficulties, culture shock, financial insecurity and lack of a support network (FERREIRA, Alisson Vinícius Silva; BORGES, Lucienne Martins, 2022; WHO, 2018).

In Ireland, a study with Brazilians revealed that many live with significant levels of stress, especially women and mothers who feel overloaded by being the pillar of the family while facing cultural and language barriers (Ribeiro et al., 2020).

⚠️ Warning signs

It is not always easy to notice that something is not right. But watch out for some signs:

● Difficulty sleeping or waking up rested

● Constant irritability or bouts of crying with no apparent reason

● Loss of motivation, loss of pleasure in simple things

● Self-deprecating thoughts or a feeling of inadequacy

● A feeling of loneliness even when surrounded by people

● Intense anxiety in the face of ordinary tasks (going to the supermarket, talking to someone, leaving the house)

These symptoms are not weakness. They are requests for help.

🧭 Pathways to support

If you recognised yourself in any of these situations, know that you are not alone — and you do not have to go through it unsupported. Here in Ireland there are resources available, in both Portuguese and English:

🌿 Support in Portuguese:

● Jigsaw (Wellbeing for Young Adults) – although in English, it offers support for young adults and usually has interpreters available.

https://jigsaw.ie/talk-online/live-chat/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=10646051693&gbraid=0AAAAADgoh_Lkn3GQPGrOmaEOHaAC2Hl7P&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5c_FBhDJARIsAIcmHK-LcSCQsv64GoMKCmZ-BnUqx6yxZ--9UbybKLXHbkkEg7lk_guxdUQaAvmKEALw_wcB

● Dublin Community Support Groups – there are informal groups of Brazilians and therapists who work online.

https://grow.ie/category/recovery-stories/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=13611074611&gbraid=0AAAAADmGKBwtsy7WFEb3_AayfRM2ZjC-3&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5c_FBhDJARIsAIcmHK8KnYFNNnYedcAMITdkJXl6XuRxYITttshrEEljeJHZrbuRBdjC2MgaAsR8EALw_wcB

🌱 Support in English:

● Mental Health Ireland https://www.mentalhealthireland.ie/

● Samaritans (free 24h call: 116 123)

● MyMind.ie – offers psychotherapy sessions at affordable prices (often with therapists who speak Portuguese) https://mymind.org/

💛 Wrapping up...

Dealing with mental health in immigration is an act of courage. It is stepping out of denial and saying: “I matter. My feelings are valid. And I deserve support.”

You do not have to be well all the time. But you can learn to be well with yourself, even on the hard days.

🗓️ Next month, we will talk about the power of support networks in the immigrant’s life:

“Building a Support Network Far from Home”. Because nobody has to walk this path alone — and when we walk it together, everything becomes lighter.

With care, Lili Fraga — Therapist and Parenting Educator www.instagram.com/lilifraga.vivaleve

como-voce-se-sente-nessa-epoca-do-ano.en_title: How Are You Feeling at This Time of Year?
como-voce-se-sente-nessa-epoca-do-ano.en_excerpt: Lili Fraga — Therapist and Parenting Educator. Seasonal Affective Disorder, the role of nature, and a meeting for the Brazilian community in Portlaoise.
como-voce-se-sente-nessa-epoca-do-ano.en_content:
Lili Fraga —

Therapist and Parenting Educator

Have you ever stopped to reflect on how your body and your emotions react to the arrival of autumn and winter here in Ireland?

Of course there are those who love the crisp cold, the silence, being tucked up in their own corner — and that is perfectly fine if it is your case. But for many of us, especially those who come from tropical countries or countries with well-defined seasons, this time of year can be challenging.

The short days, the grey sky and the constant cold affect our mood, our disposition and even our self-esteem. This has a name: what is scientifically called Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) — a type of depression related to the change of season, common in northern hemisphere countries (GUZMAN et al., 2007; SAHEER et al., 2013).

Furthermore, studies with immigrants show that the sense of isolation and low exposure to natural light amplify symptoms such as sadness, fatigue, irritability and a drop in immunity (SAHEER et al., 2013).

That is why, more than ever, this is a time to observe your own behaviour with tenderness and compassion. Recognising what affects you is the first step towards turning discomfort into care.

🌱 And what if we met?

Know that you have a real opportunity to meet other people, laugh, talk and feel part of something bigger. The Portlaoise group of Brazilians is celebrating 5 years — and to mark that beautiful journey of mutual support and connection, there will be a special in-person gathering at the park. (Event postponed; a new date will be announced).

Contact with nature and with other people is a powerful way of caring for your mental health, especially at this time of year.

Studies show that frequent exposure to green areas is directly associated with reduced anxiety and depression, as well as promoting the release of wellbeing-related hormones (TANG et al., 2023). Another survey reveals that 20 to 30 minutes in natural environments is already enough to reduce cortisol levels and increase the sense of social connection (WHO, 2021; GASCON et al., 2015).

Being outdoors, with people who share the same journey, is an invitation to welcome, to affection and to belonging.

💡 Practical tips for looking after yourself in winter:

✅ Make the most of natural light, even if only for a few minutes a day.

✅ Move your body — walks, dancing or stretching already help a great deal.

✅ Eat with intention — banana, nuts, oats and cocoa stimulate serotonin.

✅ Talk to someone — join groups, call a friend, seek therapy.

✅ Plan small weekly pleasures — a coffee, a book, a warm bath.

✅ And if you can: come to the in-person meeting! Being with other people warms the heart.

✨ Do not let winter freeze you from the inside. Let us carry on together, creating human warmth, caring for our mental health and celebrating every step of this journey away from home — but each time closer to ourselves.

📍Shall we meet at the park? It will be lovely to share this moment with you.

With care, Lili Fraga — Therapist and Parenting Educator www.instagram.com/lilifraga.vivaleve
como-voce-se-sente-nessa-epoca-do-ano.en_meta_description: How autumn and winter affect body and mind in Ireland, what Seasonal Affective Disorder is, and practical ways to care for yourself.

construindo-rede-de-apoio-longe-de-casa.en_title: Building a Support Network Far from Home
construindo-rede-de-apoio-longe-de-casa.en_excerpt: Written by: Lili Fraga — Family & Children Intercultural & Emotional Development. Connections that strengthen the immigrant’s wellbeing.
construindo-rede-de-apoio-longe-de-casa.en_content:
Written by: Lili Fraga — Family & Children Intercultural & Emotional Development

Connections that strengthen the immigrant’s wellbeing

Living outside your country of origin is already, in itself, a plunge into the unknown. But for expat mothers, the challenges multiply. Motherhood away from home carries layers of longing, tiredness, fear and, often, the temporary loss of your own identity. Who you were before you left seems distant — and now, besides being a mother, you are also an immigrant, starting from zero in a place where you do not always speak the language or understand the social dynamics.

The absence of a support network — that grandmother, that friend, that neighbour — is felt. The routine becomes heavier, rest more rare, and self-esteem can begin to weaken. The good news? Even far from home, it is possible to build new networks. Perhaps different from the ones you knew, but just as powerful, genuine and welcoming.

Help does not always appear spontaneously, and that is fine. But know this: you can find or create spaces of support that hold you emotionally, help with the challenges of daily life and remind you that you are not alone.

💡 Practical strategies for finding your network in Ireland

Here are some real and accessible ways to step out of isolation and start connecting with other people who share similar values:

👩‍👧‍👦 1. Parent & toddler groups

Community spaces where mothers (or fathers) and their small children meet to play, socialise and exchange experiences. Many are free or cost a nominal amount. 🔎 Where to find them: Family Resource Centres, local churches, nurseries or community centres. Examples: A Mother’s Embrace (Waterford), Barnardos, TUSLA parent support groups.

🤱 2. Bilingual or cultural playgroups

Joining groups that respect and celebrate your culture (such as Brazilian or Latin American mothers’ groups) helps you feel seen and welcomed. 🔎 Look for groups on WhatsApp, Facebook (“Brazilians in Ireland”, “Mothers in Dublin”, etc.) or in community schools.

☕ 3. Immigrant cafés and themed in-person meetups

Moments designed to create connections: conversation circles, workshops, wellbeing and motherhood events. 🔎 Follow local projects such as Mum talks https://www.instagram.com/mum_talks/

🧘 4. Activities that combine self-care and company

Yoga classes, walking groups, art workshops or guided meditation with other mothers. A lovely way of caring for yourself while socialising. 🔎 Search Eventbrite, Meetup or Instagram for local activities with keywords like “mothers”, “community wellness”, “creative circles”.

Some apps that can help you find the right group for you: - meetup.com- peanut-app.io- letsmush.com- nextdoor.ie

📱 5. Create your own network!

If you did not find anything that suits you, create it! A coffee morning at home with other mothers, a virtual support group and a picnic in the park. Someone is always waiting for that invitation.

💛 Wrapping up...

Connections heal. Belonging strengthens. Being seen transforms. Even far from your homeland, you can — little by little — rebuild your support network, surround yourself with people who welcome who you are today, and experience motherhood with more lightness and truth.

📌 And remember: seeking support is not selfishness. It is wisdom. You deserve to be well so that you can care — including for yourself.

Written by: Lili Fraga — Family & Children Intercultural & Emotional Development

alinhar-o-invisivel-para-harmonizar-o-co.en_title: Aligning the Invisible to Harmonise Everyday Life
alinhar-o-invisivel-para-harmonizar-o-co.en_excerpt: Text: Janine Meira Henriques. Holistic therapist, writer, playwright, artist, photographer, journalist and mother of four.
alinhar-o-invisivel-para-harmonizar-o-co.en_content:
Text: Janine Meira Henriques

Holistic therapist, writer, playwright, artist, photographer, journalist and mother of four.

Qualifications: undergraduate degrees in journalism, performing arts and holistic therapy, including reiki, radionics table work, Access bars, astrology and tarot. Psychology studies in progress, completing in June 2026.

Postgraduate studies: Brazilian literature, human sexuality.

In recent years, integrative practices that bring spirituality and personal care together have gained ground in conversations about quality of life. Among them, work with chakras and crystals stands out for combining ancestral symbolism, energetic sensitivity and an invitation to self-knowledge.

The chakras — subtle energy centres distributed along the body — have traditionally been associated with different physical, emotional and spiritual aspects of the human being. When these centres are in balance, the vital flow tends to circulate more smoothly, favouring a sense of lightness, mental clarity and emotional stability. When there are blockages, feelings of anxiety, excessive tiredness or difficulty expressing emotions may appear.

It is in this context that crystals enter as natural allies. Each stone has its own vibration, formed over thousands of years by pressure and by the elements of the earth. When placed near the body or used during moments of meditation, they can act as energetic catalysts, helping release tensions and re-establish the harmony of the chakras.

For example, rose quartz is often associated with the heart chakra, stimulating compassion, empathy and self-love. Amethyst, linked to the third eye, is seen as a support for intuition and mental serenity. Citrine, related to the solar plexus, inspires confidence and vitality.

More than a technique, aligning the chakras with crystals can be understood as a ritual of pause and presence. By dedicating a few minutes a day to breathing, feeling and observing, a person creates an inner space of listening, reconnecting with themselves and with their deepest needs.

In an accelerated world, where doing often outweighs feeling, this practice invites us to slow down and remember that balance is also born of silence, of attention and of respect for one’s own energy. After all, caring for the chakras is, in essence, caring for the life that pulses inside each of us.

If you would like to know a little more and to book an alignment session, you can get in touch on WhatsApp 085 2338910.

proposito-o-sentido-que-nos-move-por-den.en_title: Purpose: The Meaning That Moves Us from Within
proposito-o-sentido-que-nos-move-por-den.en_excerpt: Text: Juliana Gomes, founder of Escola Mulher Sistêmica. Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/juliana.mendes.gomes/
proposito-o-sentido-que-nos-move-por-den.en_content:
Text: Juliana Gomes

Founder of Escola Mulher Sistêmica

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/juliana.mendes.gomes/

I was delighted to receive the invitation from dear Tati to write for this magazine for Brazilians in Portlaoise. It is an honour to be able to share reflections on a theme as essential as it is delicate: life purpose.

My name is Juliana, I am Brazilian, I am 43 years old and I have lived in Ireland for nine years. I am Lia’s mother, Thiago’s wife and the founder of Escola Mulher Sistêmica, a school of feminine consciousness based on the Natural Laws of Cooperation of Life — laws that reconnect us to the natural cycle of existence, to ancestry and to the deep sense of belonging.

And it is precisely about meaning that I want to talk with you today.

The word “purpose” is one of the most repeated of our era. Many of us look for quick answers: What is my purpose? How do I find it?

But perhaps the truest question is a different one:

And what if purpose is not something you find, but something revealed when there is space?

Purpose is not only a mental concept. It is an intimate, spiritual and emotional perception. Especially we, women, so often overloaded by external demands, try to understand life only with the head, when purpose can only be heard with the heart.

In my experience, purpose is not confused with who we are, nor is it limited to what we do professionally. Purpose is that which moves us from within. It is a sense of direction, like an internal compass pointing to where the soul wishes to walk.

When we are aligned with that sense, life gains more harmony. But on human journeys we lose our way many times. And that happens because we live disconnected from our essence and from the natural cycle of life.

I like to think of purpose the way we think about our children: we bring them into the world, care for them, educate them, but they do not belong to us. One day they gain the world. Purpose is like that too. It is not tied to us. It needs to gain life. It is a gift given away.

Much of the emotional illness of our era is born precisely from this disconnection: burnout, anxiety, chronic stress. It is not only an excess of tasks; it is the absence of meaning in what you give.

Reconnection, however, can begin simply. A few minutes of silence. A conscious breath. A prayer. An intimate piece of writing. A sincere request to return to one’s essence.

Because it is not only what we do, but how we do it.

Sometimes the route will need to be recalculated. In some cases, the purpose is inside the current path, but with a truer “how”. In others, it will be necessary to listen to an old calling that has been waiting a long time for courage.

And it is important to remember: purpose is not a prize for those who search, but a process for those who give themselves.

May this text be only a small opening. An invitation for you to breathe and to ask yourself:

What in me wants to gain life now?

What meaning wishes to move me?

With gratitude,

Juliana

Founder of Escola Mulher Sistêmica

entre-o-silencio-do-inverno-e-o-primeiro.en_title: Between the Silence of Winter and the First Breath of Spring
entre-o-silencio-do-inverno-e-o-primeiro.en_excerpt: (February as a portal of transition) Text written by: Aria Milioni, Systemic Therapist.
entre-o-silencio-do-inverno-e-o-primeiro.en_content:
(February as a portal of transition)

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

There is a moment in the year when life seems to breathe more slowly.

It is not the height of winter, when everything has already clearly withdrawn.

Nor is it yet spring, with its open promise of movement and expansion.

February is that sensitive interval — a silent corridor between what has ended and what is

still being born.

Energetically, it is a month that disturbs deep layers.

Old emotions may reappear, tiredness becomes more visible, and a strange mixture

of impatience with apathy arises. As if one part wanted to move forward... while

another still needed to rest.

Astrologically, February usually runs through Aquarius and Pisces — archetypes of

liberation and dissolution.

Aquarius opens windows. It questions patterns, breaks old mental structures and shows what

no longer fits the version of us that is emerging.

Pisces, right after, softens the defences. It brings sensitivity and reveals where there is still

unfelt pain, unprocessed grief, forgotten dreams.

That is why February can be emotionally intense even when, on the outside, nothing

“big” happens. Inside, a great deal reorganises itself.

This is not a month of maximum productivity. It is a month of inner honesty.

In the mind, it invites us to review narratives:

— What thoughts no longer make sense for who I am today?

— What decisions do I keep postponing out of fear of changing?

In the emotions, the invitation is to feel without hurry — not to resolve everything, but to allow

old processes to complete.

In the physical body, the request is simple and therapeutic: more rest than performance, more

warmth than demand, deep breathing, gentle stretching, slow walks.

The nervous system is still in winter mode.

And winter is not a mistake of nature — it is the laboratory where the roots grow.

In the practical areas of life, February is a month of adjustment, not of expansion.

It is when we notice what really deserves energy when spring arrives — what

continues, what ends, what needs a new form.

Spring does not arrive suddenly. It begins as a whisper: one day with more light,

one deeper breath, one new idea that arises without effort.

Navigating February wisely is not forcing flowers before their time.

It is allowing yourself to:

● close cycles without dramatising

● rest without guilt

● review priorities with honesty

● release habits that no longer sustain the next version of yourself

● care for the body as fertile soil

If winter was the time to gather, February is the time to listen to what within you

wants to be born.

And when spring finally opens — inside and out — what was cared for in silence

becomes natural movement, not effort.

Perhaps the truest invitation of this month is not to do more, but to soften enough to

notice who you are becoming.

Because it is in this space between the end and the beginning that life gently decides what

your next form will be.

Aria Milioni

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

quando-a-terra-desperta-a-primavera-e-o-.en_title: When the Earth Awakens: Spring and the Astrological New Year
quando-a-terra-desperta-a-primavera-e-o-.en_excerpt: Text written by: Aria Milioni, Systemic Therapist. Astrologically this portal coincides with the Sun entering Aries — the start of the astrological New Year.
quando-a-terra-desperta-a-primavera-e-o-.en_content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

There is a moment in the year when the energy changes direction — silently, almost imperceptibly. It is like when the body wakes before the alarm and something inside you starts circulating again.

Spring begins like this.

After winter’s withdrawal, life starts pushing outwards again. The light increases, the air changes, and a natural wish arises to reorganise, to move the body and to decide what was left pending.

Astrologically, this portal coincides with the Sun entering Aries — the start of the

Astrological New Year.

If January opens the social calendar, March opens the calendar of the soul.

Aries represents the first impulse of life — the seed breaking through the soil. It does not ask for

perfection, it asks for movement. That is why, in this phase, many people feel more energy,

positive restlessness and the need to start something new.

After the dive of Pisces, which cleansed and closed cycles, the question emerges:

“And now, what are you going to do with who you have become?”

Spring is not only about flowers — it is about direction.

For mental health, this is an important period for choosing where to place your energy. The

mind wants to act, but the alignment comes from consciousness, not from excess. Ask yourself: what

really deserves my attention now?

Emotionally, the season asks for a gentle courage — allowing yourself to take up more space and

to seek relationships more aligned with who you are today.

In the physical body, Aries’ energy needs movement so that it does not turn into tension. Walking

more, stretching, returning to physical activity and receiving natural light help the nervous system leave

winter mode.

In practical life, this is the ideal moment to start projects, reorganise routines and test

new directions without demanding immediate results. It is a phase of conscious

experimentation.

Aligning yourself with the Astrological New Year is not changing everything at once, but acting from

a truer place.

If winter asked “what needs to end?”, spring asks “what deserves to be born?”

Choosing a living intention — something that can be felt in the body — is already enough to

open the way.

The Astrological New Year is an organic restart. A whisper from nature saying:

“Now you can move forward.”

The invitation is to move, without losing the inner listening that winter taught — so that action

and consciousness walk together and this new cycle is lived with presence, direction and

vitality.

Aria Milioni

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist
quando-a-terra-desperta-a-primavera-e-o-.en_meta_description: Spring and the astrological New Year: aligning with the Sun in Aries across mind, emotion, body and practical life.

📊 Laois Partnership

https://laoispartnership.ie/

Laois Partnership Company supports businesses and entrepreneurs through:

✔ rural development programmes (such as LEADER) with grants and business training

✔ SICAP, with mentoring, help with the business plan and links to support networks

✔ training and upskilling in skills that are useful for business

✔ referral to other business support organisations in Laois and the region

💡 1. Programmes and Business Information

One of the ways Laois Partnership supports businesses is through rural and community development programmes that also help local businesses grow and innovate. For example, the LEADER Programme 2023‑2027 (co-funded by the EU and the Department of Rural Development and Gaeltacht) provides financial support, training and advice for:

businesses that are developing or expanding

start‑ups that want to create new products or services

support for setting up or developing social enterprises (businesses with a social impact).

Through the programmes it implements, Laois Partnership offers or refers you to:

training in basic business skills

workshops on management, growth and sustainability

opportunities for mentoring, networking and sharing good practice

connections with other local resources and support organisations (for example, Laois Local Enterprise Office)

gestao-financeira-o-alicerce-invisivel-d.en_title: Financial Management: The Invisible Foundation of Every Business That Prospers
gestao-financeira-o-alicerce-invisivel-d.en_excerpt: By Sonia Campos, MSc in Information Science and Specialist in Business Intelligence. instagram: https://www.instagram.com/soninhafields/
gestao-financeira-o-alicerce-invisivel-d.en_content:
By Sonia Campos, MSc in Information Science and Specialist in Business Intelligence.

instagram: https://www.instagram.com/soninhafields/

Many small business owners work hard and sell well, but at the end of the month still feel that no money is ever left over. In most cases the problem is not a lack of sales, but a lack of financial organisation.

Caring for the company’s finances is not only about controlling expenses. It is about understanding where the money goes, how it comes in and how it can grow. Below are the essential points for every beginning entrepreneur:

1. Separate the company’s finances from your own.

Mixing personal money with the company’s is the most common and the most expensive mistake. When that happens:

  • The real profit becomes hard to identify

  • The cash flow gets muddled

Important decisions end up based on a feeling, not on numbers

The solution: open a separate business bank account and pay yourself a fixed salary. That guarantees clarity and security.

2. The right price is essential

It is not enough to charge “what the customer is willing to pay”. The price needs to cover:

Fixed costs (rent, bills, equipment)

Variable costs (raw materials, packaging, commissions)

Taxes

An adequate profit margin

Without this you may well be selling a lot and still losing money without noticing.

3. Profit is a tool, not a prize

When there is profit left over, many people spend it all. Solid businesses use profit to:

  • Improve processes

  • Invest in marketing

  • Buy better inputs

  • Build a financial reserve

Businesses that reinvest grow; businesses that consume everything stagnate.

4. Have a financial reserve

Problems happen. A financial reserve avoids desperation when cash is tight. It helps you to:

  • Get through weaker months

  • Avoid emergency debt

  • Make decisions without pressure

It does not have to start big, but start now, even little by little.

5. Always track the numbers

You do not need complex systems, but daily control is essential. Be clear about:

  • How much came in

  • How much went out

  • Future obligations

  • Where losses are occurring

Whoever does not track the numbers works in the dark. Whoever does, decides with confidence.

6. The biggest risk is losing money without noticing

Many entrepreneurs take in revenue but see no profit because they:

  • Price incorrectly

  • Spend without control

  • Do not track the numbers

If you feel that no money is ever left over, the problem is not how much you sell, but how you manage what comes in.

Conclusion:

Financial management is not bureaucracy, it is strategy. Entrepreneurs who understand their numbers:

  • Make better decisions

  • Reduce losses

  • Create consistent growth

If you feel you work very hard and the money is never left over, raise an URGENT flag: perhaps you are working for the sake of working, letting profit opportunities pass that could take your business to the next level.

Sonia Campos, Specialist in Business Intelligence, Consultant and University Lecturer, MSc in Information Science

Instagram @soninhafields
